activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: APY, annual percentage yield, includes the effect of compounding, so a savings rate of 4.65 percent compounded monthly is quoted as 4.75 percent APY.
story:
The line at the First Meridian branch was eleven people long, and Chloe spent most of it rehearsing what she would say. She had the brochure folded in her back pocket, the one from the community college, and she had three hundred and forty dollars in cash from the diner, and she had a plan that she had not told her father about because he would say what he always said, that money in a bank was money you couldn't touch when the furnace went.

The poster above the teller windows read, in letters as tall as her hand, that the high-yield savings account paid 4.75 percent APY. She had copied that number onto her wrist that morning, because the website had said something different. The website had said 4.65 percent, compounded monthly, and she had sat on her bed for twenty minutes trying to make the two numbers agree, certain one of them was a trick.

When her turn came, the teller was younger than Chloe expected, maybe twenty-three, with a name tag that said DENISE. Chloe slid the cash and her student ID under the glass and asked, in what she hoped was an incisive voice, why the poster and the website didn't match.

"Match how?" Denise said, counting the twenties.

"Four sixty-five. Four seventy-five. Same account."

Denise turned the brochure over, then pulled up the screen. "Four sixty-five compounded monthly," she said, reading. "That's the rate. Four seventy-five is the APY."

"What's the difference?"

"It's the APY that includes the compounding," Denise said. "Same money either way. The four seventy-five is what you'd actually get over a year." She pushed a slip across the counter for Chloe to sign. "You want it in savings, not checking?"

Chloe signed. She was still turning the numbers over, not quite able to hold them both in her hand at once, the way you couldn't hold a photograph and the person in it. But something loosened. The poster wasn't a trick. It was two ways of saying one thing, and the bigger number was the honest one, the one that told you what a year of your own money would do.

She sat in the plastic chairs by the loan desk to wait for her debit card, and that was where she overheard the man at the next desk, a big man in a work jacket, going through the terms of a truck loan with an officer. Eight thousand dollars, the officer said, and over five years the interest would bring the total to something over nine. The man kept asking him to say it again. His thumb moved along the paper like he was counting. Chloe listened without meaning to, and then with her whole attention, because the numbers were going the wrong direction. Money you owed grew the same way money you saved did, only against you, month after month, quietly, while you slept.

She thought of her father's furnace philosophy, which was really a fear of owing, and she thought of her brother Dev, who had taken out loans for a school he quit in October and now worked at the warehouse and paid them off from a paycheck that never stretched. Dev said debt was a trap that could incapacitate a person for a decade. Her father said banks were for people who already had money. And here she was with a passbook in her hand and a rate that would add maybe sixteen dollars to three hundred forty by next summer, which was nothing, which was also not nothing, because Dev's interest had started small too, just running the other way.

Her economics teacher, Mr. Farid, had once called her the class dissident, half joking, because she argued against every position they studied, including the ones she'd proposed herself. She'd taken it as a compliment then and she took it as one now. She could hold her father's fear and Dev's mistake and the poster's 4.75 percent in the same head without any of them cancelling out. Saving was slow and borrowing was expensive and both of those things were true at once, the way the rate and the APY were true at once, and a person had to look at the year, not the month, to see what was really happening.

When the card came, Denise brought it over herself. "You opening this for school?"

"Fall," Chloe said. "I'm working the summer first."

"Smart." Denise lowered her voice like she was sharing contraband. "Keep adding to it. Even twenty bucks a month. It compounds."

Chloe folded the card into her pocket next to the brochure, the paper one, the one with both numbers printed on the same page in small gray type, and walked out through the double doors into the lot where her father's truck was waiting with the engine off and the window down.

"Well?" he said.

"Four seventy-five," she said, and pulled the door handle. "Ask me in a year."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Canada's 2019 food guide suggests filling half the plate with vegetables and fruits, a quarter with protein foods and a quarter with whole grain foods.
story:
Sophie found the paper taped inside Grandma's cupboard on the first morning, right where the flour used to be. It was a photocopy of Canada's food guide, the 2019 one, with a plate drawn on it, and Grandma had pencilled a shaky arrow toward the diagram. Half the plate was vegetables and fruits, a quarter was protein foods, and the last quarter was whole grain foods. Sophie had come for the summer to help after Grandpa's funeral, expecting to mow the lawn and maybe learn to make his coffee, and instead there was this plate, waiting like an assignment.

"Sundays," Grandma said, lowering herself into the kitchen chair. "Your grandfather did the shopping on Sundays. I did the cooking. Now it's all mixed up." She rubbed her knuckles, which had swollen over the winter until the rings lived in a drawer. Sophie understood, with a feeling that was almost visceral, that the shopping list was not really about food. It was about whether Grandma could keep living in this house, in the kitchen where the ceiling fan still wobbled from the year Grandpa installed it wrong and refused to fix it.

So Sophie volunteered. She would plan a whole week of meals, buy everything on Saturday, cook in batches on Sunday, and Grandma would only have to reheat things when Sophie was at her lifeguarding shifts. It sounded simple in her head, generous even, a project she could photograph for her mother and feel good about. She made a grid on lined paper, seven columns for the days, and then she stalled, because she had never once thought about what a week of eating actually required. At home, dinner appeared. Someone else had done the invisible arithmetic.

She went back to the plate on the photocopy. Half vegetables and fruits, a quarter protein foods, a quarter whole grain foods. She turned it over in her mind the way she turned a geometry proof, testing whether it was a rule or a suggestion, and decided it was more like a ratio she could build from. If she roasted two trays of vegetables on Sunday, they could fill the big half of every plate until Friday. If she cooked a pot of barley and a pot of brown rice, that covered the whole grain quarter, though she'd have to double-check that barley counted as a whole grain, and she wrote that in the margin to look up. For the protein quarter she wrote chicken thighs, lentils, eggs, a block of tofu she'd seen Grandpa eat with evident suspicion. Then she tallied it all into a shopping list, estimating prices from memory, because Grandma had given her a budget of eighty dollars and called it, with an old-fashioned firmness, "the disbursement."

At the grocery store Sophie learned that planning and shopping were two different disciplines. The peppers she'd priced in her head were twice what they cost here; the tofu was cheaper. She stood in the frozen aisle holding a bag of mixed vegetables, and her first instinct was snobbery, that frozen was a compromise, until she turned the bag over and found the vegetables had been frozen at their peak and cost a third of the fresh ones. She changed her mind standing right there, put two bags in the cart, and felt the small shift of someone revising an opinion before it had ever really been tested. An hour later, at the checkout, the total came to seventy-one dollars and forty cents, which felt like a pardon; she had half expected to fail the budget, and the receipt seemed to exonerate her whole method.

Sunday was the batch cooking. Sophie had imagined herself competent at this, since she could scramble eggs and follow a recipe, but by ten a.m. the kitchen looked like a crime scene of peelings and she had misjudged the barley, which absorbed the water and then kept absorbing it, swelling stubbornly past the pot line. Grandma sat at the table with her bad hands folded, directing without touching. "More oil on the second tray. Your grandfather never used enough oil and then he wondered why the carrots tasted like penance." Sophie laughed so hard she had to set down the knife.

It was during the afternoon lull, while the lentils burbled, that the subtext surfaced. Grandma had been watching Sophie arrange containers in the freezer, labeling them with masking tape, and she said, very evenly, "You'll be at the pool until six on Tuesdays and Thursdays." Sophie said yes. Grandma said, "So I'll be doing the reheating myself." It wasn't a question, and underneath it Sophie heard something she hadn't planned for: Grandma was negotiating how much help she could accept without feeling managed, the same way Grandpa had negotiated the ceiling fan, badly installed but installed by him. Sophie could have pointed out the obvious, that the microwave had large buttons, that the containers were stackable. Instead she said, "Could you write me a note about which ones you want on which days? You know what you like better than I do." Grandma's shoulders came down half an inch, and she reached for the pencil.

They ate the first meal together at the small table by the window, chicken and barley and a mountain of roasted peppers and zucchini. Sophie looked at her plate and did the math without meaning to: the vegetables took up half, the chicken a quarter, the barley the last quarter, and she felt a quiet click of satisfaction, that a fact from a photocopied page had become an actual dinner. She was honest enough with herself to admit what stayed uncertain. She didn't know if she'd be bored of peppers by Thursday, or whether the frozen ones would be watery, or whether eighty dollars would hold for a second week when the lentils ran out. The guide didn't say anything about loneliness either, or about a grandmother eating alone on a Tuesday. Those were problems the plate couldn't solve.

"More zucchini?" Grandma asked, already reaching with her bad hand for the serving bowl before Sophie could answer.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A metronome marking of 60 means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second.
story:
The band room smelled like valve oil and the ghost of thirty years of cafeteria disinfectant, and Logan had forty minutes before Mr. Reyes came back to hear him play the solo. He set the metronome on the music stand, dialed it up to 144, and attacked the passage. It collapsed by the fourth bar, his fingers tangling on the D to E-flat shift, the clarinet squawking like something stepped on. He tried again. Worse. A junior named Priya looked up from her flute in the corner and said nothing, which was somehow louder than laughing.

"You're choking it," she said finally.

"I'm fine. It's the reed."

"It's you." She came over, picked up the metronome, and spun the dial all the way down. "Sixty means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second. Try it there."

"That's half speed. Reyes will hear half speed."

"Reyes isn't here yet."

Logan took the clarinet back and played the passage at sixty, one note per second, and it was ugly in a different way, so slow he could hear every small fault he'd been hiding inside the fast blur. His embouchure sagged on the long tones. His thumb lifted too early. It was like hearing a recording of his own voice and wanting to deny its veracity, except the metronome didn't lie, and neither, apparently, did Priya.

"I sound like a dying goose," he said.

"A dying goose with good fingerings, though. That's progress." She tapped the stand. "Again."

The all-state audition was in eleven days. He'd told his father he had a real shot, and his father had asked whether that was true or whether Logan was doing the thing he did, the optimistic thing, and Logan had said true, and now he wasn't sure, and now he had to be sure in eleven days, and the crepuscular light through the band room's high windows made the whole problem look exactly as gray as it felt. He played the passage again at sixty. Again. On the fifth try something happened: the notes stopped being a race and became a shape, and the shape had a logic, and his fingers learned where they wanted to go before he told them.

Then Priya bumped the dial up to 80 without asking, expropriating control of his practice session like it was hers, and he almost said something, but he played it, and it held. She took it to 96. It held. By the time the hallway clock showed 4:15, he was back at 144 and the passage ran clean, not perfect, but clean, and he sat back and breathed like he'd surfaced from deep water.

"You're welcome," Priya said.

"You hijacked my metronome."

"You were going to fail gloriously at full speed instead of succeeding boringly at half speed. Somebody had to intervene." She packed her flute into its case, snapping the latches. "The question is whether you'll slow down again tomorrow when nobody's watching, or whether your ego will decide it's cured."

Logan looked at the metronome, still ticking away at 144 like a small smug heartbeat. His father's question was the same question, really, wearing different clothes. He didn't know the answer. He dialed it back down to 60 and watched the pendulum swing, one beat per second, slow as honesty.

Mr. Reyes came in at 4:20 with a coffee and his usual expression of a man perpetually arriving somewhere more important. "Show me the solo."

Logan raised the clarinet. He didn't tell Reyes about the sixty, or the eleven days, or the dying goose. He just set the metronome ticking, and played.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
story:
The portal refreshed itself at 3:04, and Florence refreshed it again at 3:07, though the email had said decisions would post by five o'clock and nothing about the page had changed except the advertisement for a webinar on financing, which rotated every ninety seconds like a metronome for her panic. The application deadline had been the first of November, submitted at 11:41 the night before, and she had been waiting three weeks now, which was long enough for hope to extrude itself into something thin and fibrous, something she could no longer hold without its shape collapsing.

"You're staring at it," her brother Dara said from the doorway, still in his soccer shorts, tracking mud in small crescents across the hall tile. "It's not a microwave. Staring doesn't make it finish faster."

"I know that." She pulled her hands into her sleeves. "I'm not staring. I'm checking."

"You're staring." He came in anyway and leaned on the back of her chair, and she let him, because Dara was the only person in the house who understood that the waiting had a physical weight, that it sat on her sternum in the afternoons. He had waited for his own decisions two years ago and refused, afterward, to tell anyone which schools he'd even applied to, which she'd understood at the time as privacy and understood now as something closer to mercy.

She scrolled up to the test score section, though she had it memorized. The digital SAT she'd taken in March, the new one, at the rec center with forty other kids on borrowed laptops. She'd been calm through the first math module, calm in a way that almost frightened her, and then the second module had opened and the questions were harder, denser, word problems wearing disguises, and she had spent the last twenty minutes convinced she was failing. She'd typed her answers with cold fingers and walked out certain, and then the score had come back higher than any practice test she'd taken, and she had not told anyone, not even Dara, that she didn't understand why.

She called Priya at 3:20 because Priya had taken it the same day, same room, two rows over.

"You're doing the refresh thing," Priya said, instead of hello.

"The refresh thing, yes. Also I need to ask you something and you can't laugh." Florence pulled her knees up onto the chair. "The second math module, in March. Did yours get harder than the first one?"

"Obviously. That's the whole point. It's adaptive." There was the sound of Priya's dog being pushed off a bed. "The digital SAT switched to that format in March. How you do on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second one."

Florence was quiet for a second. "So if the second module was harder, that means..."

"That you did well on the first. They don't waste hard questions on people who bombed the easy ones. I spent the whole second module grinning like an idiot because it was brutal, and I figured brutal meant I'd earned it." Priya laughed, a short sound. "Wait. You didn't know this? You took it in March."

"I thought I was drowning," Florence said. "I thought they'd figured out I was a fraud and were finishing me off. I almost cancelled my score in the parking lot." She pressed her palm flat against her forehead. "I got a good score and I spent a month believing it was an accident."

"You're a connoisseur of worrying," Priya said. "You've refined it into an art form. Most people just worry. You curate."

Florence laughed, and then the laugh bent into something else, and she held the phone tighter. "That's the thing, though. That's what I've been doing all day. The portal's going to say yes or no and I'm already writing both stories. In one I get in and it's a mistake, some tangential error in the file, and in June somebody notices and emails me a retraction. In the other I don't get in and it confirms what I already know. I've been doing this since I was twelve, Priya. I did it with the swim team. I do it with every grade."

"So don't do it now," Priya said, simply, as if Florence had merely forgotten where she'd set her keys.

"That's not how it works."

"I know. Okay. Here's what we do. You close the laptop until five. Not refreshing, closed. And whatever it says, you call me before you tell anyone else, before you even decide what it means. Deal?"

"Deal," Florence said, though she did not close the laptop, and Priya knew she wouldn't, and let her keep it.

At 4:51 Dara brought her a mug of tea she didn't ask for and set it down on the coaster their mother would have nagged about. At 4:58 she refreshed. The page went white for four full seconds, long enough for her to hear the refrigerator cycling in the kitchen and Dara breathing behind her, and then the page rebuilt itself with a banner she had never seen before, blue, with her legal name in it, and she read the first line twice because the words would not arrange themselves into sense on the first pass. Dara put one hand on her shoulder without reading over her, waiting.

She picked up her phone and dialed. "Priya. It's up."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
The fountain at Meridian Park had a ring of wet stones around it, and Eli had chosen a bench fifteen feet away because it was close enough to hear the water but far enough that they would have to lean in to talk. He had been sitting there for nine minutes, phone face down on his knee, rehearsing openers. Before tonight he would have said he was reticent by nature, but reticence, he was learning, was a thing you could perform rather than a thing you were, and performing it for an hour seemed like a disaster.

Junie arrived on a bicycle, one hand waving, the other steering badly. She braked too late, hopped off, and dropped her chainless bag on the grass, and a water bottle rolled out and knocked over the iced coffee he had bought her, the one he'd carried across the park balanced on a napkin like an offering. Ice and brown liquid spread across the concrete. She stood over it with her hands half raised, as if the spill might be reversible.

"That's it," she said. "The whole evening is cursed. I've known you for four minutes and I've already destroyed your property."

"It's a coffee," Eli said. "It's three dollars of coffee."

"It's an omen." She crouched and gathered the napkins he handed her, pressing them into the puddle, which only smeared it wider. "I do this. I'm a clumsy person on important days. It's like the universe files it under highlight reel."

He almost said it wasn't important, which would have been a lie, and he almost said it was fine, which would have been nothing. Instead he said, "There's this thing my brother told me about. In 1966, Elliot Aronson ran an experiment with a quiz contestant who was really good, like clearly competent, and the guy spilled a cup of coffee. People rated him more likable afterward, not less."

Junie looked up from the puddle. "You made that up to be nice."

"I didn't, actually. It's called the pratfall effect." He heard how it sounded, a term dropped like a coin on concrete, and kept going anyway. "I only know it because my brother took a psych class and repeats everything from it at dinner. But it's real. The spill helps, if people already think you're good."

"So I accidentally deployed a strategy." She balled the napkins and missed the trash can by a foot, and neither of them moved to pick them up. "Fine. New rule for tonight. Every clumsy thing I do, you tell me it's science."

They walked the loop around the pond because sitting still was worse than moving. He learned that she had transferred schools in October, that she kept a list of birds she'd seen in the park and had only nine entries because she kept losing the list, that she wanted to study something she called the phenomenology of ordinary things, which she had to explain twice, and which he understood on the second try as the study of how a thing feels from inside, like the difference between a pond and your pond. He told her about his brother leaving for college in August, and how the house already felt like it was rehearsing his absence, and she didn't say anything comforting, which he preferred.

At the duck pond she tried to point out a heron and knocked his own drink into the grass. This time they both laughed, and he thought about how the effect his brother described couldn't be the whole story, because the spill wasn't what he liked. He liked that she had stopped apologizing by the third stumble and started narrating them instead, calling them data. But he couldn't separate the two cleanly, the clumsiness from the person, and he suspected nobody could, and that this was either the point of the experiment or the thing it missed. He kept all of that to himself and drank nothing.

They ended back at the fountain because the light was going and the bench was where they'd started. She sat with her knees up, and he sat a careful six inches away, and she said her mother was picking her up at the parking lot in ten minutes, and the ten minutes started immediately feeling shorter than ten minutes.

"I'm going to text you," he said. "Unless that violates something."

"It violates nothing." She was quiet for a moment, picking at the strap of her bag. "Here's the honest part. I liked tonight. But I'm bad at knowing if I like someone or if I like that they listened to me talk about phenomenology for an hour. Those feel the same from the inside."

"They don't have to be different yet," Eli said, surprising himself, and meaning it, and being unsure.

She smiled at that, or at the fountain, and stood, and her bike, which she had leaned against the bench, chose that exact moment to fall over with a clang. She looked at it, then at him, and held out her hand for the verdict.

"Science," he said.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The standard tuning note is A above middle C at 440 hertz, formalized by the International Organization for Standardization as ISO 16.
story:
I am not the kind of person who gets nervous, which is why my hands were perfectly steady when I carried the trumpet case into the community center on Tuesday nights. My uncle had left the trumpet to me in his will, along with a note that said only "learn it," and since he had never explained anything in his life, I didn't see why death should change him. I had been coming to the Thursday beginners' band for six weeks now, and I was, I would say, improving, though Mr. Okafor the director had a way of saying "closer" that suggested a distance I preferred not to measure.

The band tuned before every rehearsal. Mr. Okafor would hold up his phone, tap a tuner app, and a thin, pure note would fill the multipurpose room, bouncing off the basketball hoops and the folded cafeteria tables. Everyone hummed or played along, forty instruments at once, all of them, in my experience, wrong in different directions. My trumpet was reliably flat. I knew this because the app, when I played into it, showed my A drifting below the little green line like a fish sinking.

That was how I learned the note had a name and a number. A girl named Priya, who played clarinet and sat beside me partly because the seating chart was alphabetical and partly, I suspected, because she pitied me, saw me squinting at the phone. "It's A four forty," she said. "A above middle C, four forty hertz." She turned her clarinet over in her lap. "There's a whole standard for it. ISO sixteen. Some international organization decided that's what A means." I said that seemed like a lot of ceremony for one note, and she said everything worthwhile has a lot of ceremony around it, and I pretended I hadn't heard, because the alternative was admitting she was right.

Here is what I couldn't stop wondering, though I kept it to myself for two more weeks: if a committee had to decide what A was, then before the committee, what was it? Every orchestra, every bedroom guitarist, tuning by ear to each other in the dark, and none of them wrong exactly, just not agreed. The question metastasized through my practising. I would be working through the C scale in my bedroom, and suddenly I would be thinking about whether the note I was playing existed or was only a consensus, and my embouchure would fall apart and the trumpet would make its sad elephant sound, the one my neighbor had already complained about in a passive-aggressive note taped to my door.

The trouble came to a head at the winter showcase rehearsal. Mr. Okafor announced that we would perform in three weeks, the whole band, in front of actual humans, and then he raised his phone and gave us the A. I played mine, and the app showed flat, as always, and I pulled my main tuning slide out a bit the way he had shown me, which raises the pitch, and played again. Closer. Still under. I pulled again. Then Priya, who was having a morose evening because her reed had cracked, said without looking at me, "You're going to pull that slide right off the trumpet."

I told her I wanted to be exactly on the line. She said, "It's a reference, not a judge." I said a standard was a standard, and she said, "It's an agreement, Jake. It's so we can be together, not so we can be perfect," and I want to be honest that this annoyed me, partly because she was probably right and partly because I had spent three weeks building a whole philosophy around that little green line, and philosophies don't like being deflated in one sentence. It felt like bathos, honestly, a grand question about the nature of sound collapsing into a cracked reed and a girl telling me to stop fidgeting with my slide.

But she had put something in my head that wouldn't leave. All through the rehearsal, while we mangled a simplified arrangement of "Ode to Joy," I kept noticing that when we were slightly off, all of us, off in the same direction, it didn't sound bad. It sounded like an orchestra warming up, like a room full of people breathing. When one person was off alone, that was the fish sinking. Maybe the point of the four forty was never the four forty. Maybe the point was that everyone held the same note in their mouth at the same time and listened for each other, and the number was just the excuse to listen.

I tested this, quietly, during the break. I asked Mr. Okafor if I could see his phone, and I played my A against it, adjusting until the needle finally, finally settled on the line, and I stood there for a second feeling the small triumph of it. Then I asked Priya to play her A, and she did, and I matched her instead of the phone, and the two notes locked together with a faint wobble in them, like the sound itself was breathing. I don't know which one was more correct. I genuinely don't. The phone was certain and Priya was warm and I stood between them holding a trumpet my dead uncle had told me to learn.

At the showcase, three weeks later, I was not nervous, as I have mentioned, which is why I had to keep wiping my palms on my trousers backstage. The band filed out under the fluorescent lights, forty of us and about sixty audience members, mostly parents and one man who appeared to be there for the free coffee. Mr. Okafor raised his phone to give us the A, tapped the app, and nothing happened. The screen stayed dark. He tapped again. He turned the phone over, removed the case, blew on the charging port like it was an old cartridge. The room waited. Somebody in the second row coughed.

And then Priya, without asking anyone, put her clarinet to her mouth and played the note herself, long and steady, an A she had been hearing every Thursday for months, and one by one we all came to her, strings and brass and the wheezy flutes, until the whole band was humming around her single reed like bees around a queen. Mr. Okafor lowered his dead phone and looked at us, and I could not read his face at all. We were, I am fairly sure, not at four forty. Nobody in that room knew where we were. The man with the coffee put down his cup, and we began.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The game started at one, and by one-fifteen Morgan was wedged between the good couch and her cousin Denny's elbow, holding a plate of her grandmother's deviled eggs she didn't want. The room smelled like onion dip and radiator dust. Every chair in the house had been dragged in from the kitchen, the porch, the sewing room, because her grandfather had invited the whole block, profligate with his invitations the way he was with everything except the thermostat, which he kept at sixty-four.

Her younger cousin Theo, who was nine, sat on the carpet with his chin on the coffee table. On third down the running back swept right and the camera followed him, and Theo pointed at the screen. "That's the line," he said. "The yellow one. They repaint it every play."

Morgan looked at the field. The yellow stripe sat across the grass, ten yards past the ball, and when the camera cut to the sideline angle it was still there, crisp as tape. She had watched games in this room since she was Theo's age and had never once thought about it. "They repaint it every play," she repeated. "Between plays. In thirty seconds."

"They have guys," Theo said. "With sprayers."

"Nobody's running out there with sprayers." Denny laughed without looking up from his phone. "It's painted on before the game."

"It can't be," Morgan said, mostly to herself, because the line moved. It was always ten yards ahead of wherever the ball was, and the ball moved, and the camera moved above it all, and a painted stripe would end up crooked on the screen, tilted, running uphill whenever the camera panned. This one stayed level. It lay flat against the grass no matter where the camera went, like it belonged to the picture and not to the field. She worked through it while the crowd on TV roared at a tackle she didn't see. "It's not on the grass at all," she said. "It's on the broadcast."

Theo turned around on his knees. "What does that mean, on the broadcast?"

"It means it's drawn on top, like a filter. Like the arrows they put on replays." She reached over him for her grandmother's laptop, which lived on the side table next to the bowl of peppermints. Her grandfather had wifi now, one of his few concessions to the century, and she typed in the words while Denny said, in the voice he used for everyone, "Morgan, it's a game, not a thesis."

The search came up fast. The line was computer-drawn, drawn into the video before it reached anybody's television. It had first been broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, and a company called Sportvision had done it. She read the date twice. Her grandfather had been fifty-one. Theo's mother hadn't been out of high school. There had been a whole history of football on TV before the line existed, decades of it, and everyone had just looked at the field and done the arithmetic in their heads.

"It's not painted," she told Theo, and turned the laptop so he could see. "It's computer-drawn. The first time it was on TV was ESPN, September 27, 1998. A company called Sportvision did it." Theo studied the screen with his mouth slightly open, the way he looked at the fish tank at the dentist's office.

"So where does the yellow go when the players walk over it?"

"Nowhere. They're really walking over plain grass. The yellow isn't down there with them."

That was the part Theo couldn't let go of, and she couldn't entirely either. The players stepped on the line and their cleats sank into real turf and the yellow lay untouched on top of it, and something about that arrangement made her feel like she'd been handed a small machine with its back panel off. "So the TV knows where the first down is?" Theo asked. "The TV is doing math?"

"Something's doing math," Morgan said. That was as far as she could take it honestly. How the picture kept track of the grass, how it knew green from white from a referee's knee, she couldn't say, and she wasn't going to guess at it out loud in front of Denny, who was waiting for exactly that.

The room had gone quiet in the way it did when her grandfather decided something was interesting. He leaned forward with his hands on his knees. "Nineteen ninety-eight," he said. "That's the year we put the deck on. I watched games on a little television out there on sawhorses." He looked at the screen for a while, at the yellow stripe holding its ground while a punt sailed over it. "Whole first half of my life without that line, and now I'd be lost without it."

"It invigorates the whole thing," Denny's father said from the kitchen doorway, raising his glass. "Couldn't follow a down before that thing came along."

Theo stayed on the carpet through the next series, watching not the receiver but the stripe itself, and every time the ball was placed he announced the new line before it appeared, which he got right twice and wrong once. Morgan kept the laptop open on her knees. The game went on. On fourth down, with the crowd noise climbing, Theo tugged her sleeve.

"When they didn't have the line," he said, "how did you know where they had to get to?"

Morgan looked at the field, at the yellow band sitting on grass it had never touched. "I don't know," she said. "I guess they just knew."

fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
The mailbox at the end of the driveway still had the red flag up from yesterday, though the mail had already come and gone. Emma stood in front of it with her mother's coffee thermos in one hand, breathing fog into the cold, and tried to decide whether opening the little door counted as an action or a delay of one.

Nothing inside except a furniture catalog and a postcard from the dentist. She had known that, probably. The decisions from her two remaining colleges wouldn't come by mail for another week, and even then they'd come online first, but she kept checking the box anyway, the way you keep pressing a bruise to confirm it's still there.

Back in the kitchen her younger brother Danny was doing homework at the counter, and her mother was on the phone with her aunt in the living room, the door half open. Emma sat down across from Danny and pulled the folded printout from her back pocket: the list she'd made in October, seven colleges, now crossed down to two.

"Which one's the fake one," Danny said, without looking up.

"Neither." She flattened the page. One was Alden, a small school two states away that had sent her a brochure with a photo of a girl rowing at dawn. The other was Marlowe, the state university, where half her class was already going. She'd been treating the choice as settled, in a way, telling people she'd be happy either way, and the tellings had started to calcify into something like belief, a shell over the question she'd stopped actually asking.

But the question was still there, and it had a shape now. In December she'd been on a forum late at night, scrolling through threads about financial aid, and she'd found a word she hadn't known: need-blind. Someone had written, "Alden is need-blind, Marlowe is need-aware for out-of-state but not in-state," and Emma had read it four times before it opened. Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay. Many US colleges are instead need-aware. She'd sat with her knees pulled up in the desk chair, feeling the sentence rearrange things. Marlowe, the affordable one, the sensible one, might have looked at her parents' income when it decided. Alden, the reach school, the expensive one, had not. It seemed backwards, and then it didn't, and then she wasn't sure, which was where she'd stayed for a month.

"I don't get why you care," Danny said now, actually looking at her. "You applied already. It's done."

"Because it means they wanted me, maybe. If they take me." She tapped the Alden line on the page. "If a school is need-blind, they said yes or no without knowing we're broke. And if they said yes, the yes is just a yes. It's not, we like you but also, can you pay?"

"That's the nerdiest thing about being wanted I've ever heard."

"You're fourteen. Everything sounds nerdy to you."

Their mother came in still holding the phone, pressing it to her chest. "Aunt Rosa wants to know if you've heard anything."

"Next week, probably. Tuesday."

"Both of them?"

"Both." Emma folded the list again, smaller this time, until it was a hard little square. Her mother went back to the call, and through the half-open door Emma heard her say, "No, Marlowe makes more sense, you know, with the money," and something in Emma's chest went both warm and tight at once, because her mother said it so gently, like a fact about weather.

Here was the thing she couldn't make linear: the money was real. If Alden took her, there would be loans, or there wouldn't, depending on aid nobody could predict yet. Her mother's math was honest, and so was Emma's wanting, and they pointed in different directions, and she was tired of pretending that wanting didn't count just because you couldn't put it in a spreadsheet. She wasn't going to be blasé about Alden the way some kids at school were about their fifth-choice safety; she'd earned the specific, unglamorous hope of it. But she also couldn't pretend the choice was only about hope. Both things were true at once, and holding them together made her feel less decided, not more, and she was beginning to suspect that was not a failure of thinking but the actual shape of it.

She took her coffee back outside. The mailbox flag was still up, stupidly, signaling to nobody, and she pushed it down with one finger until it clicked. Then she stood there a moment longer, looking down the street where the mail truck would come on Tuesday, and she made herself one small deal: she would open both letters, whatever they were, before she told Danny or her mother or Aunt Rosa a single word about either one. First she would know. Then she would decide, or she would sit in the not-knowing a little longer, honestly, with the list still folded in her pocket.

The truck turned the corner at the far end of the block, a day early, stopping and starting along the curbs. Emma watched it come, thermos warming her hands, and did not move until it had passed her house.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel.
story:
The garage smelled of cut grass and old gasoline, and Camille had claimed it as hers for the summer mostly because no one else wanted it. Her grandfather's keyboard sat against the far wall beneath a shelf of coffee cans, and beside it, on a wooden stool she'd dusted twice, sat the metronome. It was a pyramid of walnut with a brass pendulum, and she had wound it the first night out of curiosity, then spent twenty minutes just listening to it divide the silence.

She was eighteen and had wanted, for reasons she couldn't fully defend, to learn the piano before college began in the fall. Her mother called it a late start, which was true, and her friends called it a personality trait, which was crueler. Camille herself thought of it as a sabbatical from being good at things. Four years of cross country and honors chemistry had left her fluent only in achievement, and she wanted, before the dorms and the syllabi, to be bad at something on purpose.

The problem was the left hand. Her right could pluck out a melody from the beginner book well enough, but her left lagged behind, and when she tried to bring them together the whole thing collapsed. So she turned to the metronome, set it slow, sixty beats a minute, and tried to make her hands obey. They wouldn't. She slowed it to fifty, then forty, and at forty she could do it, but the tempo felt like a walker, like physical therapy, and she stopped out of humiliation even though it worked.

Her grandfather came out on a Sunday with two glasses of iced tea and lowered himself onto an overturned milk crate. He didn't teach; she'd asked him not to. He only listened while she played the same eight measures four times, and after the fourth he reached over and set the sliding weight a little higher on the pendulum. She missed the changeover immediately, both hands tangling, and glared at him.

"You did that on purpose."

"I got it in Amsterdam in 1971," he said, which was not an answer. "A man in a shop told me Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, though the design was really Dietrich Winkel's. Maelzel took the credit. Winkel had the idea." He sipped his tea. "I've always liked knowing that. The thing keeps perfect time and its own history doesn't."

Camille looked at the pendulum, ticking away in its patient, indifferent rhythm, and understood that it didn't care who had made it or who got the credit for making it. That was the part she liked too. It simply delimited the silence into pieces small enough that her hands could agree on them, and whether she found that mercy or tyranny depended, she was discovering, on the minute.

She tried the eight measures again and made it through six before failing. She tried again. On the fifth attempt she stopped watching her hands and listened instead to the tick, letting it hold the tempo so she didn't have to, and the passage happened, all eight measures, clumsy but whole, and her grandfather raised his glass a half inch off his knee.

The cost arrived on schedule. She had wanted the summer to be a place outside her usual life, somewhere unmeasured, and now she found she was timing herself against the fall. Forty days until move-in, and she was converting practice sessions into progress like units, and the pleasure of being bad at something was becoming a plan to get less bad, which was only her old life wearing a new uniform. She asked her grandfather, that evening, whether he thought it was tenable, learning an instrument this late, whether it could actually go anywhere.

"Tenable," he repeated, like he was tasting the word. "You want to know if it can hold weight." He stood, knees cracking, and pushed the sliding weight up a few more notches, faster than she had ever set it, and set the pendulum swinging. "Sit down. Play."

She sat. The tick came at her quick and bright, and her hands went for it and missed, and went for it again.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
The portal refreshed itself at 3:14 on a Thursday afternoon, and Keira watched the little wheel spin the way she imagined people once watched roulette. When the page loaded, the word was not "Congratulations" and not the flat gray of denial. It was "Waitlist," rendered in an unbothered navy blue, as if the college were merely suggesting she take a number.

She read the letter twice, then called her grandmother into the room, which was unfair, because Gran had been hoping all week for a reason to stop scrubbing the grout. "It means they liked me," Keira said, "but not enough." Gran squinted at the screen. "It means you're a backup date for the prom, sweetheart." Keira groaned, but she was already scrolling to the FAQ, where she learned that waitlist spots are filled in May, after admitted students have sent their deposits and the college knows how many places are still open. She said this out loud, slowly, and Gran patted her shoulder and said the pasta would not boil itself.

The trouble was Ridgemont, the safety school she actually liked, whose own deposit deadline sat there on her desk calendar like a smug little toll booth, due in April. Four hundred dollars to hold a place she might not need. She did the math on a napkin: four hundred dollars was eleven weeks of bagging groceries at Horvath's, where the break room smelled permanently of onion and the manager's stories about his fantasy football league had, over two years, begun to enthrall her against her will, the way a slow leak enthralls a bucket.

Her brother Dev found her at the kitchen table with three browser windows open and the napkin. "You look like a conspiracy person," he said, stealing a cracker. "I'm a person with a decision," she said. "There's a difference." He leaned over her shoulder while she showed him the numbers, the May waitlist movement, the April deposit deadline, the gap between them like a plank across a moat. "So you'd pay Ridgemont to save yourself, and then if the other one calls, you burn the four hundred."

"Basically."

"Grand. You're gambling four hundred dollars on a college that ranked you 'maybe.'"

She threw a cracker at him, and he caught it in his mouth, which ruined the gesture entirely.

That night she opened a blank document, which was what she did when a problem refused to behave. At school, Ms. Amara had once called her essays "tangential," and Keira had decided to take it as a compliment: she followed a thought wherever it led. So she made two columns. One said PAY. Under it she wrote: a guaranteed room somewhere she liked fine, parents not worrying, senior spring without a sword hanging over it. The other said WAIT, and under that she wrote the name of the first college, and then nothing, because everything she wanted to put there was a feeling, not a fact, and she was trying, for once, to be a person who noticed the difference.

But the columns refused to stay separate. She caught herself arguing across them like two lawyers who secretly agreed. The first school had enticed her with its physics department and its absurd gothic library, but Ridgemont had a co-op program and a professor whose lecture on entropy she had watched, voluntarily, twice, laughing alone at his joke about disorder always winning because it had more players. Was the first school worth four hundred dollars of pure uncertainty, or was she in love with a building? Her mother's voice drifted up from downstairs, complaining to Gran that nothing in the house stayed where you put it, and Keira thought, not for the first time, that entropy was a family condition.

She typed a sentence at the bottom of the document: I don't know if I want it more, or if I just want to be wanted. Then she deleted it, then she typed it again, because it was true even if it was embarrassing. The honest position, she decided, was this: she would pay the deposit, because a bird in the hand was not a cliché when the hand had earned the money one onion-scented shift at a time, and she would stay on the waitlist, because wanting something did not become disloyal just because she'd bought insurance. Both things could be true. She would not pretend the four hundred dollars didn't sting, and she would not pretend she'd stopped hoping.

In May, after deposits everywhere had settled and the colleges counted their openings, she refreshed the portal at 3:14 on a Thursday, purely from superstition. The wheel spun. Dev appeared behind her with two forks and a bag of leftover pasta, which he offered without a word, held out like a peace treaty or a wager. The page began to load.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it acts mainly as a feedback: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like carbon dioxide.
story:
The trail climbed out of the pines into a clearing where the whole valley opened up, gray-blue and hazy, and Mr. Okonkwo's voice finally gave out behind them. He had insisted the debate team practice outdoors, saying that a change of venue extenuated the staleness of their arguments, whatever that meant, and so eight of them had followed him up the switchbacks with water bottles and printed evidence packets sweating inside their backpacks.

Coralie walked beside Dennis, who had drawn the skeptic's position in tomorrow's scrimmage. That was the assignment, to argue that the case for carbon dioxide was overstated, and Dennis took assignments seriously, which was the trouble with him. For two miles he had been rehearsing his opening under his breath like a prayer he didn't believe in.

"Water vapor," he said suddenly, aloud this time. "There it is. Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas. That's my whole first rebuttal. If water vapor traps heat, and there's more of it than anything else, then CO2 is a side character. That's the argument. That's what they use."

"That's what who uses?" Coralie asked, though she knew. She had seen the clip he'd found, some man in a suit holding up a graph.

"Everyone who says CO2 doesn't matter." Dennis stopped at the trail's edge, where a wooden sign with a faded map showed their elevation in peeling numerals. "Look, I'm not saying I believe it. But I have to argue it tomorrow, and I don't actually know why it's wrong. Do you?"

She didn't, she realized, which galled her, because she was the one on the team who cared about this. She had given a speech in April about the Keeling curve, the sawtoothed line of carbon dioxide climbing across a century, and she had described it beautifully without understanding what made the sawtooth, why the line dipped each year and rose again, always higher than before. She had said "seasonal respiration" and moved on quickly, hoping no one would ask.

They sat on a flat rock below the sign and she pulled out her phone, which had one bar. Dennis leaned over her shoulder, smelling of sunscreen and trail dust. She found the graph first, the full record, and they looked at it together, the little wobbles riding on the long climb. Then she typed water vapor into the search field and started reading, slowly, out loud, stopping whenever she hit a sentence she couldn't say like she meant it.

"Okay," she said after a while. "So it's true. Water vapor really is the most abundant greenhouse gas. Your clip isn't lying about that part."

"Ha," said Dennis.

"But listen. Warmer air holds more water vapor." She read the line twice because it seemed too simple. "So when something else warms the air, the air pulls in more water vapor, and that traps more heat, which warms it further. It's not the trigger. It's the amplifier." She looked up. "It's a feedback. That's the word they use."

"Feedback," Dennis repeated. "Like a microphone next to a speaker."

"Kind of. The point is the warming starts with something else. With gases like carbon dioxide. Water vapor just makes whatever CO2 starts into something bigger." She scrolled down, checking, because she wanted to be sure before she said it to him. "So your whole rebuttal is true and it doesn't matter. It's the most abundant, and it's still not the cause."

Dennis was quiet for a moment, watching a hawk tilt over the far ridge. "That's actually a better argument against me than anything Priya's going to say tomorrow," he said. "She'll just call me a denier."

Below them on the switchback, Priya herself came around the bend, red-faced and cheerful, with Marcus behind her arguing about whether their coach counted as a mentor or a tormentor. Priya flopped onto the rock beside Coralie, looked at the graph still glowing on the phone, and said, "Is that the CO2 curve? God, it's so ugly when you zoom out. Like a hockey stick having a seizure."

"That's the sawtooth," Coralie said, and then, because Priya was actually asking, she tried to explain it, the breathing of the northern forests, and found she could almost do it now, the way you can almost play a song you've only heard while trying to teach it.

"You two are disgustingly sagacious for a Thursday," Marcus said, dropping his pack. "Meanwhile I got lost twice and Mr. Okonkwo called me a navigational embarrassment."

Coralie smiled, but she was still turning something over. She thought about how she'd built her April speech, all that certainty, that rising line, and how she'd stood in front of the room and implied she understood things she'd only memorized. There was a kind of consanguinity between her speech and the man in Dennis's video, she thought, an actual family resemblance: both of them using a true number to say something the number couldn't carry alone. She hadn't lied. She had just never gone down into the basement of her own facts and checked the supports.

"So what do I do tomorrow," Dennis said. He wasn't joking now. "I still have the assignment."

"Argue it. Argue it the best you can, that's the drill." She paused. "But when they counter you, don't fight the water vapor thing. Concede it fast and keep moving. If you fight it, you'll lose the room."

Mr. Okonkwo's voice floated up from below, calling them onward to the overlook. They shouldered their packs. Dennis lingered a second, zipping the packet away, and said, quietly, "For the record, I made my cousin send me that clip. I wanted a rebuttal I couldn't beat, so I'd know I'd beaten everything."

She stared at him. "You've known the answer since Tuesday?"

"I knew the answer. I didn't know the why until just now, up here, from you." He tightened a strap and started up the trail. "That's why I asked you and not Google."

She stood a moment in the clearing, phone warm in her hand, uncertain whether she'd been taught something or used, and then she followed him toward the overlook, where the rest of the team was already shouting at the view.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Ray Oldenburg's 1989 book The Great Good Place named 'third places', such as cafes and libraries, where people meet outside home and work.
story:
The last box in Nicolas's room was labeled MISC, which his mother said was a way of admitting you had no idea what you owned. He sat on the bare mattress and texted Devon: you coming or what. Devon replied with a thumbs up and, three minutes later, appeared in the doorway holding two energy drinks like an offering.

They spent the afternoon doing nothing much in a room that was already nobody's. Devon peeled the labels off the cans in long strips. Nicolas stacked the boxes by size and then restacked them by weight, which made no difference to anything. When Devon left, he said, "It's only two hours away," and Nicolas said, "I know," and neither of them said the thing that underpinned the whole visit, which was that two hours was far enough to turn friends into memories you scheduled around.

The new town revealed itself in stages: a highway exit with three gas stations, a main street that pretended it hadn't been designed for cars, and a library built of pale brick with a plaque from some civic club nobody had belonged to since the seventies. They had no internet hooked up yet at the apartment, which was his mother's excuse and his reason. On the third day he walked there with his laptop and no real plan.

He chose a table near the periodicals because it had a window behind it and an outlet underneath, the way a hermit crab chooses a shell. A girl was already at the next table with a textbook open to a diagram of a cell, highlighting it in a color he had never seen used for anything, a kind of acid green. She looked up once, looked down, and that was the extent of their diplomacy for an hour.

He came back the next afternoon. And the one after. The girl was there both days, always alone, always highlighting as though the diagram would eventually confess something. On the fourth day a man with a beret and a chessboard set up at the table by the magazines and waited, and within ten minutes an older woman arrived, unzipped her own board, and they argued over whose to use. This happened every day. Nicolas began to feel like a wildlife observer.

"You're the table guy," the girl said on Friday, when he dropped his charger cord and she caught it before it hit the floor.

"I'm the table guy," he said. "You're the cell girl."

"Mitosis, actually." She capped the highlighter. "My grandmother does the chess thing too. She calls this her office. She retired and couldn't stand the house."

"It's not an office."

"She means it like that. Not home, not work." She shrugged, as though the rest were obvious. "Some sociologist wrote a whole book about it. The Great Good Place, 1989, guy named Ray Oldenburg. He called them third places. Cafes, libraries, wherever people meet outside home and work."

"Third places," Nicolas repeated, and the phrase settled somewhere with the satisfaction of a key fitting a lock that he hadn't known was locked.

He thought about Devon then, about the two of them orbiting a convenience store parking lot for four years, and about how the parking lot had never mattered and had mattered entirely. He had been mourning the wrong thing. It wasn't Devon specifically, though it was also Devon specifically. It was that in the old town he had never once had to build a place to stand; the standing places had been handed to him, pre-made, underpinned by other people's routines. Here nobody's routine included him yet. That was the actual problem, and it was, he noticed with some surprise, a solvable kind of problem, or at least a workable one.

"You want to know something embarrassing?" he said. "I've been telling my mom I come here for the wifi."

"Is that not true?"

"The wifi is bad. The wifi is a lie we tell each other." He felt the grandiose version of the speech forming in his head, something about loneliness and architecture and how cities fail their eighteen-year-olds, and he let it die unspoken, because she had a cell diagram to finish and he had, he realized, a small and sufficient errand. He got up, walked to the magazine table, and stood over the chess game.

The man in the beret glanced up. "You play?"

"Badly," Nicolas said.

"Sit down, then. Ludmila here needs humbling."

"From a child," Ludmila said, already sliding the board to make room.

The girl with the highlighter watched from her table, and Nicolas thought about texting Devon later: found a third place, there's this old woman who trash talks in two languages. His phone stayed in his pocket. He sat, took the white pieces without ceremony, and moved a pawn into the center of the board.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 Lancet paper claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism described just twelve children, and The Lancet fully retracted it in 2010.
story:
Brayden found the printout folded in his jacket pocket during fourth period, where it had been since his uncle Ray had pressed it on him in the clinic waiting room on Tuesday. His mother was there for her blood pressure, and Uncle Ray had come along because he liked the free coffee, and somewhere between the vending machines and the examination rooms he had produced the article from his coat as though handing over evidence in a trial. "Read that," he had said. "Twelve kids. Twelve, and they wrote it up in that Lancet paper like it was the word of God." Brayden had taken it to be polite, and now, in the back of Ms. Ferreira's classroom, he smoothed it flat under his chemistry binder and looked at it properly for the first time.

The room smelled like the ethanol Ms. Ferreira used to wipe the whiteboards, and the radiator under the window ticked in its slow, patient way. On the front table sat the day's materials: a folder of journal abstracts she had photocopied for their unit on how scientific knowledge actually gets made. Brayden had taken the class because it counted for his last science credit and because the alternative was physics, which he had already survived once. He had not expected the unit to have anything to do with his uncle.

"Okay," Ms. Ferreira said, pulling a stool to the front. "You've all got the abstracts. Three different studies, same question. Talk to each other. I'm going to sit here and drink my coffee and say nothing, which will be harder for me than for you." A few people laughed. She held up her mug as if taking an oath.

Brayden's partner was Priya Raman, who wanted to be an epidemiologist and said so to anyone who would listen, and to several people who would not. She had already spread her three abstracts in a row like playing cards. "So these two find the same thing," she said, tapping two of them, "and this one finds nothing. But it's a bigger sample, so I trust it more, but the other two agree with each other, so." She spread her hands, palms up, the gesture of someone offering a problem rather than a conclusion.

"One study finds something and two don't," Brayden said slowly. He was still thinking about the folded article. "What if there's just one study? Just the one, and it's the only one anybody ever reads?"

"Then you're in trouble," Priya said. "Unless somebody repeats it. That's the whole point, right, that's what she keeps saying. It doesn't count until somebody else does it and gets the same answer, and then somebody else after that." She pulled her sleeve over her wrist, a habit of hers. "Why, do you have a one-study situation?"

He almost said no. Instead he unfolded the article on the table between them, and she leaned in, and he watched her eyes move down the page. "My uncle gave me this at the doctor's office," he said. "It's about that Lancet thing. The vaccine thing. It says twelve children."

Priya sat back. "The Lancet retracted it," she said. "In 2010. Fully retracted. That's not a small thing, they don't do that lightly."

"It doesn't say that in here anywhere."

"No," she said. "It wouldn't, would it."

Brayden turned the page over, then back, as if the retraction might be hiding on the other side of some fold. Twelve children. He had a sudden clear memory of Uncle Ray's face in the clinic's fluorescent light, certain and generous at once, a man handing his nephew a shield. And it occurred to Brayden that he had been halfway to believing it, not because the science was convincing but because Uncle Ray was, and that these were two different kinds of trust and he had been sliding between them without noticing.

He raised his hand, which surprised him. "Ms. Ferreira. What happens to a paper that gets retracted? Does everyone who read it find out?"

She took a long sip of coffee, visibly wrestling with her vow of silence, and lost. "That, Brayden, is one of the best questions in this whole unit, and I'm going to answer it with another question. You found that article somewhere. Is the retraction easier to find or harder to find than the article was?" Then she set the mug down and pointed at the abstracts. "Priya, keep going. You two are circling something."

They worked through the rest of the period. Priya explained peer review the way she explained everything, fast and with her whole face, and Brayden listened while a suspicion assembled itself in him piece by piece: that Uncle Ray was not a liar and not a fool, that he was something harder to be angry at, an apologist for a story he had needed once and could not now put down. Brayden had seen him on the family group chat, patient and then suddenly vitriolic, defending the article against cousins who sent him links. Brayden had scrolled past all of it. He had never once asked where any of it came from.

When the bell rang, Priya packed her cards of abstracts and said, "Look it up tonight. The retraction. Then text me what you find, because if your uncle's version is out there, other people's uncles have it too." She shouldered her bag and was gone into the hallway noise before he could answer.

He walked home the long way, past the clinic, and stood outside it for a minute with his hands in his pockets. His uncle had sat in that waiting room drinking free coffee and being wrong in a way that felt, to him, like love. Brayden could not disabuse him with a fact the way you'd take away a sharp object, and he did not want to ambush him with a link the way the cousins did. He took out his phone and opened a message to Uncle Ray and typed, "Can I ask you something about that article," and then sat on the low wall by the clinic steps, thumb hovering, watching the automatic doors slide open and shut for people going in.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky's 1988 book Manufacturing Consent argued that news is shaped by five 'filters', the first of which is the ownership of media by large corporations.
story:
The book came from the college library downtown, three weeks before Olivia's summer class ended, and she read it in the living room because it was the only room with air conditioning. Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky's 1988 book Manufacturing Consent argued that news is shaped by five filters, and Olivia had copied that sentence into her notebook on the bus, the pen jolting against the page. The first filter, the book said, was the ownership of media by large corporations. She had underlined it twice, then felt embarrassed by the underlining and tried to erase one of the lines, which only smeared the paper gray.

Her assignment was to take one local news story and trace it through two outlets. She had chosen the story about the mill closing out past Route 9, four hundred jobs, because her uncle Denny had worked there for eleven years and because both papers had covered it. On the living room carpet she spread the clippings side by side. The Clarion's version ran three paragraphs and led with the company's statement about restructuring. The other paper, the Valley Courier, ran nine paragraphs, named the union rep, printed the number of jobs in the headline. Olivia wrote these observations down. Then she turned the clippings over and looked at the mastheads, and found the Clarion's parent company listed in small type, and looked that company up on her phone, and found that the same corporation also owned the plant's mortgage holder. She sat with that for a while. The ceiling fan clicked on its third rotation, a sound she had never noticed before.

Marcus came over at four with his laptop because they were supposed to draft the piece together. He was the kind of student their teacher called a polymath, the one who had taught himself to suture a wound at fifteen after a cycling accident, and who now kept a first-aid kit in his backpack for other people. He dropped onto the couch and read her notes upside down.

"So you're saying they buried it because of who owns them," he said.

"I'm not saying that," Olivia said. "I'm saying the book's first filter is ownership. I can't prove why the Clarion ran three paragraphs."

"That's a weak thesis."

"It's an honest one."

They argued through the crepuscular hour, the windows going from gold to gray, Marcus tapping the arm of the couch, Olivia refusing to write the sentence he wanted, the one that said the paper had protected its owner. She could not know that. She could only know who owned what, and that the coverage was different, and that the difference had a shape to it.

Across town, in a kitchen that smelled of burned rice, Denny read his niece's text twice. She had sent him the Clarion clipping and asked what he thought of the coverage. He thought about the union rep the Clarion never called, the way the photographer had come to the gate on the last day and taken pictures of the sign and not the men. He thought about telling her all of that. He typed instead that the story was fine, deleted it, typed that the story was fine, and sent it before he could change his mind again. Some things a man carried on his own. His wife watched him set the phone face down next to his plate, and she did not ask, because in eleven years she had learned which silences to leave alone.

Back in the living room, Marcus had given up on the strong thesis and was formatting the citations while Olivia held her phone, her uncle's message open on the screen. "Fine," he had written. Nothing else. She read it the way she had read the mastheads, looking for the small type.

"Marcus," she said. "Two-sentence conclusion. One: the outlets are owned by different companies. Two: the coverage differed. Three: the book's first filter says ownership can shape news, and this story is consistent with that, but it doesn't prove it."

"That's three sentences."

"Fold two into one." She picked up the clipping with the mill gate in it, the workers small in the background, and set it on top of the stack. "I'm keeping the picture, though. The Clarion didn't run this one."

He looked at the photo, then at her, and started typing.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A population pyramid conventionally shows males on the left and females on the right, with age groups stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top.
story:
Mr. Osei had left the classroom door propped open with a wedge of folded cardboard, and the corridor smell of floor wax drifted in and settled over the desks. Noah sat near the window, where the afternoon light made a long rectangle across his worksheet, and on the worksheet was a chart he did not understand. It was a profile of Kenya, printed from some atlas, two columns of horizontal bars standing back to back like shoulders pressed together, and beneath it the question: Will this country need more schools or more nursing homes in thirty years? Explain your reasoning.

He had a reason, and it was wrong. He had decided the wide bars at the top of the chart meant crowds of children, so the answer was schools, plenty of schools, and he had written half a paragraph before Priya leaned over from the next desk and said, "You've got it upside down." He looked at her, then at the chart, then back. "It's a pyramid," he said. "The point goes up."

"Flip it," she said. "Youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top." She tapped the wide base of the shape. "All that is down here. That's the young ones." She was eating a cereal bar in small bites, holding it in her left hand so the fingers of her right stayed clean for her own worksheet. "And males on the left, females on the right, by the way. That part matters if the imbalance is at one age."

Noah erased his paragraph. The rubber smeared graphite into a grey bloom across the paper, and he turned the sheet over and started again on the blank side, because the front was no longer trustworthy. He copied the bars with his pencil, quickly, to feel their shape in his hand: a broad base tapering steeply to a narrow tip, a country stacked with young people at the bottom of the chart and thinning out toward the old ones at the top. Schools, then. Still schools. But now the answer felt different, because he had arrived at it by a road he could see rather than a guess he had dressed up as a guess he hadn't made.

His phone buzzed against his thigh, and he angled it below the desk. A message from his sister Amara, who was on a gap year in Warsaw and owed him letters she never sent.

"Visited a travel agency today to book a bus ticket," she had written. "They had country profiles on the wall, little charts, and I stood there reading one upside down for a full minute before the agent laughed at me. Bars are ages, apparently. Kids at the bottom, grandparents at the top. I felt like an idiot. Also I met a girl who works at a care home and she says they can't fill the jobs. Love you, learn something."

He typed back, "I'm literally learning that exact chart right now," and put the phone face down on his knee. He noticed that his own first mistake, made twenty minutes ago in a classroom, was the same mistake his sister had made in a travel agency in Poland, and that this comforted him in a way he didn't examine too closely. People misread the same things everywhere. The bars ran the way they ran regardless of who was looking.

Priya was working on Japan, her chart an almost perfect rectangle with a slight pinch in the middle. "Nursing homes," she said, not looking up. "Obviously." Mr. Osei passed between the desks with his hands behind his back, paused at her sheet, and said only, "Consider what you might be leaving out," and moved on. Noah watched Pria's jaw tighten. She hated being told to consider things. She began writing fast, and he could see the word migration appear twice, underlined.

That word sat in Noah's mind while he drew his own Kenya again. The bars showed the population as it stood today, stacked youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top, males on the left half and females on the right. But the question asked about thirty years from now, and thirty years from now the children at the base would be the adults in the middle, having or not having children of their own, leaving for Dubai or London or not leaving, and no chart on the page could tell him which. He thought of the care worker in Warsaw who couldn't be replaced, and of his uncle, furloughed from the cement plant two winters ago, who had said at dinner that a man who loses his shift loses his whole shape. He thought about how a population, unlike a fact, was ductile; you could bend it with work or war or a new highway, and it would hold the bend.

He wrote his answer in careful sentences. The base of the pyramid was broad, so schools first, certainly schools. But he added a paragraph beginning "What I cannot know from this chart is," and in it he put migration, and policy, and the possibility that the whole shape could be bent in a decade by decisions nobody had made yet. He did not pretend this was a failure of the chart. He wrote that the chart was honest about the present and silent about the future, and that a person reading it had to admit which half of the question was arithmetic and which half was weather.

When the bell rang, Priya was still writing, and Mr. Osei stood at the doorway collecting nothing, watching them file out. Noah stopped beside him with his worksheet folded once. "I got it backwards at first," he said. "The whole thing. Read it like a tree, oldest rings inside." Mr. Osei took the sheet, glanced at the paragraph that began with what Noah could not know, and handed it back. "Keep that part," he said. "Most people abrogate the uncertainty the moment they find a number that looks solid." Noah slid the paper into his folder, between a history handout and the permission slip for Thursday's trip, and followed the others out into the corridor, where the wax smell was already giving way to rain coming through the open doors.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: ATP synthase works like a tiny rotary motor: protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP.
story:
Brandon spread the textbook on the picnic table and pinned it open with two rocks from the flowerbed, because the August wind kept flipping the pages back to glycolysis as if the chapter itself wanted him to start over. Tomorrow was the placement exam, the one that would decide whether he entered freshman biology or spent a semester in remedial science, and though he had told his mother it didn't matter either way, he had not believed himself when he said it.

He read the pathway aloud, half to the yard and half to nobody: glucose, broken in the cytoplasm, pyruvate carried inward, the citric acid turning and turning and yielding almost nothing he could hold onto. The words slid past him the way names did on the first day of a job.
