Somewhere in there, at the end of all of it, sat the mitochondria, and inside them a thing the book called the electron transport chain, and beyond that a molecule called ATP, and the exam expected him to trace the whole route from sugar to energy without once getting lost.

The problem was that he had never been good at this and had chosen it anyway. Last spring, when his counselor asked why he wanted to switch from the vocational track to pre-med, he had said something about liking science, which was only partly true. He liked the idea of it, the way it dichotomized the world into things you could verify and things you merely believed, and after his junior year, when his father's diagnosis had come and gone in a blur of words like "idiopathic," he had wanted to live somewhere that words had to prove themselves. Whether that was a real reason or an extrinsic one, a story he told to make the choice look noble, he still couldn't say.

A screen door banged and Deja came out carrying two glasses of lemonade, ice already melting fast in the heat. She had been his lab partner in the one honors class he'd risked, and she was starting at the state university in nine days, and she had agreed to quiz him today mostly, he suspected, so they would have one more afternoon before everything scattered. She sat on the table's edge, set the glasses down, and said, "Okay. Glucose goes in. Then what."

He got as far as the inner membrane and stalled. Deja didn't prompt him. She watched a june bug crawl along the table's splintered rim with the patience of someone who had learned, in a year of shared labs, to let him find his own way out of a silence. And in the silence he was suddenly not in the backyard at all but at the science museum in sixth grade, the one field trip his father had chaperoned before the diagnosis, standing in front of a giant plastic enzyme with a rotor in the middle. The placard had said ATP synthase. A guide had spun the rotor with his hand, and the other kids had gotten bored and wandered toward the dinosaur hall, but Brandon had stayed, and his father had stayed with him, reading the little sign twice through his glasses.

"Protons," Brandon said now, slowly. "Protons flow through it, through ATP synthase, and they make part of the enzyme spin. Like a motor. It actually spins, and the spinning is what builds the ATP." He heard how it sounded, like a claim a person should be embarrassed to make about something smaller than a cell, and Deja laughed, but not at him. She said, "Yes. It's literally a rotary motor. That's the part everyone gets wrong on the exam, they think it's just a metaphor." She drew it on a napkin with a pencil stub from her shirt pocket, a lollipop shape with a hole through the stem and an arrow showing the protons pouring through, and the rotor turning, and the ATP coming off the top.

What struck him, sitting there with the wind riffling the napkin's edge, was that his two versions of the world, the one he wanted to save for and the one his father had stood beside him in, had stopped being opposites the moment he said the sentence out loud. He had spent a year trying to dichotomize them less, and here the work was already done for him: the motor was real, verifiable, and it was also the most beautiful thing he had ever been asked to memorize. His discernment, such as it was, told him that the first thing he'd loved about science was not the rigor but the spinning model with his father's breath fogging the glass case, and that both of those could be true, and that he could not yet tell which one would still be there in November.

Deja was saying something about the shuttle proteins, and he turned the napkin over and asked her to start again from glucose, and he went through the whole path twice, all the way to the little motor at the end. When she left at dusk, she took the textbook but left him the napkin, folded into his shirt pocket without comment. Later, in the kitchen light spilling across the grass, he unfolded it by the picnic table and looked at the lollipop shape, then noticed, for the first time, in his father's handwriting in the bottom corner, small and faded, three words he had no memory of the man putting there: held up fine.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A home with a 1 percent yearly flood chance has about a 26 percent chance of flooding at least once during a 30-year mortgage.
story:
The trail climbed out of the parking lot through a stand of boreal spruce, dark and resinous, the kind of woods that held its cold an hour after the fields below had warmed. Alexis walked behind his father and ahead of Marcus, who was telling them, again, about the house he'd closed on two days ago. "Three bedrooms, and the yard goes right down to the water," Marcus said. "You can hear the river from the porch."

Alexis had his tablet zipped into the front of his pack, and in his head he had the deadline. The city council had opened a comment period on the riverside rezoning, and it closed at five o'clock tonight. His geography teacher had not assigned it; she had merely mentioned it, and Alexis had decided that if he was going to learn to use the mapping software properly, he ought to use it on something real. By noon he had pulled the floodplain layer over the parcel map of the city, color-coded so that anything with a yearly flood chance of one percent showed up green. Then Marcus had called, wanting company on the hike, and Alexis had brought the tablet along with the plan of finishing his comment at the summit, where there was supposed to be signal.

"How far to the top?" Marcus asked, ducking under a dead limb.

"Forty minutes, maybe," Alexis's father said. "Less if you stop narrating the house."

Marcus laughed, but Alexis noticed how he described it. The river as an amenity. The porch. The price per square foot, which was, Alexis had thought even then, suspiciously good.

They stopped at a granite shelf where the trees opened. Wind moved through the spruce with a sound like distant surf, and Alexis took out the tablet, shielding the screen glare with his jacket. The overlay was all there, the layers cached offline: parcels, flood zones, and a third layer he'd added himself, median income by block, because he wanted to see not just where the water would go but who would be standing in it. He worked the zoom with two fingers until the map found the river's southern bend, and there, outlined in green, was the new subdivision. He tapped the parcel records and read the owner's name. He read it twice.

"What are you doing up here, anyway?" his father asked, crouching beside him. "You've been staring at that thing since the car."

"School thing," Alexis said. He angled the screen away, casual, though his pulse had picked up. The parcel database was public, but it still felt like reading someone's mail. He pulled up the comment draft and typed fast, the cold making his fingers clumsy. One bar of signal flickered at the top of the screen and then vanished, like something surfaced from deep water and gone again.

"Let the boy breathe," Marcus said, dropping onto the granite with a granola bar. "Tell me about this school thing, though. You're mapping floods? They teach you that in tenth grade now?"

Alexis looked at him. Marcus was forty-three, had spent his savings on the down payment, and was unwrapping his granola bar with the untroubled contentment of a man who believes his luck has finally turned. Alexis thought about what his grandfather used to say, that school should inculcate not just facts but the habit of checking them. He had always found the phrase stiff. Now he understood it as a kind of mercy, or a kind of cruelty, depending on which side of the check you were standing.

"It's not really floods," Alexis said. "It's odds." He turned the tablet so Marcus could see the green polygons riding the river. "A home with a one percent yearly flood chance has about a twenty-six percent chance of flooding at least once during a thirty-year mortgage." He said it evenly, the way you'd read a weather report, and watched Marcus's jaw slow on the granola bar.

"Twenty-six," Marcus repeated. "That's over the whole mortgage."

"That's over thirty years. And you got a thirty-year, right?" Alexis didn't wait for the answer. He pulled the signal meter up again. Nothing. The comment box sat on the screen, cursor blinking after the sentence about the southern bend, which he had not yet typed. He could submit it without the parcel name. He could submit it with it. His father was watching him now too, having gone quiet in a way that Alexis recognized from arguments at the dinner table, the way his father went quiet when he wanted Alexis to arrive somewhere on his own.

Alexis typed the name of the subdivision. He typed that the city's own data placed it inside the one percent zone, and that the people buying there were, on the block-level income layer, measurably poorer than the people on the hillside two miles north. He did not type Marcus's name. He did not know yet whether that was honesty or cowardice, whether the veracity of a public record was worth more than the privacy of a friend, and the comment box waited under his hands like a question with more than one right answer. Two bars of signal appeared, held. His thumb hovered over submit. Marcus leaned over and read the screen upside down, and after a long moment, in a voice Alexis hadn't heard from him before, said, "Press it."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
story:
Oliver pulled the roasting pan from the oven at four minutes past five, holding it in folded towels the way his mother used to hold his sister when she was small, close and careful, and set it on the stovetop. The thermometer in his phone app said the beef had hit 125 degrees, exactly the number the recipe called for, and he felt something in his chest loosen for the first time since Tuesday.

His sister Nadia sat at the counter with her chemistry homework, watching him with the dour expression she had worn since the custody schedule was finalized. "You're doing Dad's recipe," she said.

"I'm doing a recipe." He slid the probe out and covered the roast with foil. "Sit down. It'll be ten minutes."

"Since when do you cook?"

Since their father's Sunday dinners stopped existing, he didn't say. Since their mother's new shift schedule left the kitchen empty at the hour it used to smell like rosemary. Instead he washed his hands and began the potatoes, and the two of them worked in the silence of people who used to talk more.

The ten minutes passed. When Oliver carved into the roast, the center had gone from the pink he'd aimed at to a flat, uniform gray-brown, and the juices ran thin instead of gathering dark on the board. Nadia leaned over his shoulder. "That's overcooked."

"I took it out at exactly the right temperature." He said it flatly, defensive, and then hated the sound of it. He sat down on the kitchen stool and looked at the app again, at the graph of the temperature over time, as if the numbers owed him an apology.

Then he remembered his father, one Sunday last spring, pulling a rib roast out early while their mother protested it was still cold inside. Dad, it's raw. No, it's resting. Oliver had thought it was superstition then, the kind of kitchen folklore adults passed around like weather predictions. Now he typed into his phone with his thumb: why did roast overcook after leaving oven.

The result came up fast. He read it twice, then a third time, because it contradicted something he'd believed about cooking all evening. "It's called carryover cooking," he said out loud, mostly to himself. "The food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat. A big roast like this can go up several degrees while it rests."

"So the recipe was wrong?"

"The recipe was right and I was wrong." He turned the phone so she could see the page. "It gave me the target temperature. It didn't tell me to stop before the target. I hit 125 in the oven, and then the resting did the rest of it." He laughed once, short and not quite amused. "I interpolated. I took the number I was given and filled in everything around it with my own assumptions."

Nadia pulled the phone closer and read for a while. "So next time you take it out low and let it climb."

"Next time." He looked at the gray meat on the board, at the foil still holding a little trapped heat, and thought about how he had watched the app climb toward 125 with such certainty, such trust in the single number, and how the whole time the roast had been carrying its own arithmetic forward without him.

Their mother came in at six, coat still on, and stopped at the smell of it. "You cooked."

"Dad's roast," Nadia said, before Oliver could stop her, and their mother's face did something complicated that settled into a careful neutral.

"It came out overcooked," Oliver said, standing. "First attempt. I'll get it right."

They ate anyway, the three of them, at the table with the good cloth that hadn't come out since spring. The meat was dry and Nadia drowned hers in horseradish, and their mother said it was good twice, the second time more sincerely, and Oliver found that being angry at a fact was useless in a way being angry at a person wasn't. A roast wasn't trying to deceive him. It just kept going after he thought he was finished with it.

"So you'd take it out at like 118," Nadia said, fork in the air, working it through. "And trust the rest."

"Trust the rest," Oliver said. "Which is, I know, basically an oxymoron coming from me." He'd spent four months refusing to trust anything that happened after things ended, after the boxes were packed, after his father's apartment stopped feeling like a place they were visiting and started feeling like the other half of their lives.

Later, alone in the kitchen, he wrapped the leftovers and set the app to build a graph for next Sunday: pull temperature 118, projected climb of several degrees, resting time twenty minutes. The projection line rose gently after the oven went dark, the way nothing in his life had been allowed to lately. He looked at it for a long moment, then typed a title at the top of the screen. Attempt two.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, the closest relatives of the person who died sit shiva, a mourning period of seven days that begins after the burial; the Hebrew word shiva means seven.
story:
The mirrors in Grandmother's house were covered with sheets, and Arianna kept catching herself looking for her reflection anyway, finding only white cloth and the dim shape of the hallway behind it. She had arrived the night before the burial, straight from packing her dorm room into three boxes, and now the boxes sat in the trunk of her car outside while she sat on a low wooden stool in the living room, which was what her grandfather had told her to do. "We sit shiva now," he had said. "After the burial, seven days. The word means seven." Then he had gone into the kitchen and not come out for an hour.

The problem was orientation. Her college ran a mandatory advising session on Thursday, which was day three, three hours away by train, and her mother had offered a noncommittal shrug when Arianna asked whether she should go. "It's your education," her mother said, which was the kind of answer that handed the decision back to you like a plate you didn't order. Arianna had spent the whole year sharpening herself into someone practical, someone who could argue that grief was a chemical state and mourning a technology for managing it, a small private rationalism she'd built from philosophy podcasts and her own refusal to cry at the hospital. By that logic she should go to orientation. By that logic the stools and the covered mirrors were mechanisms too, just older ones, and she could take or leave them.

People came all afternoon. They brought casseroles and coffee cakes and plastic containers of things nobody would ever finish, and they said "I'm sorry" and then stood in the kitchen talking about parking. Around four the doorbell rang and it was Priya, from her calculus class, holding a paper bag with both hands like it might bolt. "I didn't know what to bring," Priya said. "My mom said food, but my mom also said don't ask questions, which was helpful."

"Food is right," Arianna said. "You can put it on the counter with the other twelve coffee cakes."

Priya set down the bag, which contained, it turned out, another coffee cake, and they both laughed at that, quietly, and then Priya sat down next to her on the couch and didn't say anything for a while, which Arianna understood was the correct thing, though she hadn't known it was correct until someone did it.

Her grandfather came out of the kitchen eventually and lowered himself onto a stool and told a story about Grandmother insisting on renting the same lake cabin eleven summers in a row, and how he had tried to extenuate the expense with a spreadsheet, and how she had looked at the spreadsheet and then at him and said, "Some things you don't get to make smaller." Everyone in the room nodded, and Arianna felt something shift in her chest that she did not want to examine yet, because examining things was how she made them smaller, and maybe that was the point of the stools, of sitting low, of seven whole days in a house with the mirrors covered: you didn't get to make it smaller, you had to sit inside the actual size of it.

That night she asked her uncle to drive her to the train station in the morning. She had reasoned it through, or told herself she had, but at the station she stood on the platform with her ticket in her hand and watched the board flip from ON TIME to DELAYED, and then to DELAYED again, forty minutes, and she thought about her grandfather alone on his stool while the house emptied out, and she thought about Grandmother's spreadsheet, and she walked back to the parking lot before the train came. Her uncle raised an eyebrow. "Changed your mind," she said, and he drove her back without comment, which was its own kind of mercy.

On day seven, the last day, Priya came by again with a bag of clementines because she'd decided coffee cakes were a failed genre. The house was loud with cousins and the smell of the brisket Aunt Renata had insisted on cooking even though everyone said they weren't hungry, and everyone ate it anyway. Somebody uncovered one mirror and left the others for later, and Arianna caught her reflection in the hallway, blurry and unfamiliar, older somehow, or maybe just less arranged. Her grandfather found her standing there.

"So," he said. "You missed your advising session. You'll have to make it up."

"I emailed them," she said. "I told them I was sitting shiva. Seven days, starts after the burial. The girl at the office said, 'What's shiva?' and I said, 'It means seven,' and she said, 'That's not an explanation,' and I said, 'I know.'"

Her grandfather laughed, a real one, the first since the funeral. "And what did you tell her instead?"

"That I'd explain everything Thursday," Arianna said, "when I'm back on campus." She peeled a clementine, split it, and handed him half through the doorway.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Winston Churchill said in a speech at Fulton, Missouri, on March 5, 1946, that an iron curtain had descended across Europe.
story:
The county library smelled of carpet cleaner and old paper, and by four o'clock the afternoon light came through the tall windows in long bars that Hunter kept walking through on his way between shelves. He had four books spread across a study table, two of them fat histories of the Cold War, one slim, and one his grandfather had pressed on him at dinner last Sunday, saying that a man named Gaddis had settled the whole question decades ago. The question, apparently, was whose fault the Cold War was, and Hunter's history teacher had asked the class to take one side by Friday, with evidence. Hunter did not want a side. He wanted the thing itself, whatever it was, the way you want to see the bottom of a pool before you jump.

The first historian, the one his grandfather liked, wrote as if the answer were obvious. Stalin wanted security and got paranoia, or wanted paranoia and got security; either way, the Soviet Union moved first and moved hard, and the West merely reacted. The second historian spread the blame thinner, almost elegantly, like butter taken too far and tearing the bread. Both of them cited the same events, which was what unsettled Hunter most. The same speeches, the same summits, bent to opposite purposes, as though the facts were wet clay and each writer had a different thumb.

His reverie broke when Priya dropped her bag on the other end of the table and started unpacking highlighters with the seriousness of a surgeon laying out instruments. She was in his class and had chosen the other side, the one that put more weight on American actions, and they had agreed, in a loose and wary way, to work in the same room without helping each other.

"Did you get to the Churchill thing," she said, not quite a question.

"There's a Churchill thing in both books."

"Both books quote the speech," Priya said. "But the historian I'm reading says it was in Missouri, and yours says it was in England. One of them is wrong, or they're both being sloppy." She slid her book across, and Hunter slid his back, and the two sentences sat there like witnesses giving slightly different addresses for the same house. One thing they agreed on: the year, 1946, and the month, March.

Hunter went to the reference desk, where a laminated card listed the databases, and then to a terminal in the corner whose fan rattled like a small animal in the wall. He typed the sentence he half remembered from the books, the one about the curtain. The database returned a transcript, and there it was: Fulton, Missouri, March 5, 1946. A small college town in the middle of the country, not London, not Westminster, nothing grand. He sat back. It should not have mattered so much, the where, but it did, because the British historian had placed the speech in the wrong country and then built half a paragraph on that imagined setting, calling it a homecoming delivered to a war-weary London crowd. Hunter wrote the details on an index card in his small, careful hand: Fulton, Missouri, March 5, 1946, the speech where Churchill said an iron curtain had descended across Europe. He underlined nothing. Underlining felt like taking sides.

He carried the card back to the table and set it between Priya's book and his own, neutral territory. "The one who got the venue wrong also got the argument wrong," he said. "Or maybe he wanted the argument and then found the venue." He was thinking out loud, and he could hear how unsure it sounded. The American historian, the one his grandfather called definitive, had used the speech the other way, as proof of a clear-eyed warning the West ignored at its peril. But if the same speech could serve both masters, then the speech was not proof of anything except that a former prime minister, putative prophet or retired politician depending on who you read, had been invited to a small college in Missouri and said something memorable. Hunter found that he did not know what it proved, and that not knowing felt like standing on a floor that was, at last, solid, because at least he could see it.

Priya turned the card over, as if the date might be printed twice with a correction on the back. "So I can't use my guy for this part," she said. "He quotes it right, but he quotes it the way you quote scripture, like the words did the work instead of the tanks."

"Mine does it too," Hunter said. "He just does it in the other direction." He pulled a fresh sheet of paper and ruled two columns, then a third narrow one down the middle, and labeled them. In the first column he wrote what the evidence actually showed, the things both historians had to admit. In the second he wrote what each claimed the evidence meant, side by side, so the claims could look at each other. The third column he left almost empty, and at the top he wrote one word: unsolved. He would turn that in on Friday, he decided, not as a failure but as the honest shape of the thing, and he would argue not for one side but for the difference between what happened and what the tellers of it wanted.

The lights over the stacks clicked to half brightness, the library's signal that evening had started without them. Priya capped her last highlighter and leaned over to read his columns. "You're going to get marked down for that middle one," she said.

"Probably," Hunter said, and slid the iron curtain card to the top of the page, where the facts could keep watch.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: For Mexico's Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2, families build home altars called ofrendas with orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are believed to guide souls home.
story:
The cultural center smelled of cempasúchil before Jackson even reached the door, the orange marigolds crowded in buckets along the entryway, their scent thick enough to lean on. His mother carried the framed photograph wrapped in a dish towel, the way she carried things she considered breakable in more than the obvious sense. His grandfather had been gone since March, and tonight, the first of November, the family would set his picture on the ofrenda for the first time.

Inside, the hall had been transformed by folding tables draped in white and purple paper, each one holding somebody's dead. Jackson moved past altars crowded with sugar skulls and clay dishes and old letters, trying not to read too closely, though it was hard not to. A woman was arranging pan de muerto in a careful spiral. Two kids argued over whose grandmother's candles were crooked.

"Where do you want him?" his mother asked. She had chosen a spot near the window, where the afternoon light came in slanted and gold. The family altar, she explained to his younger cousin, was called an ofrenda, and theirs would be modest this year because they were still learning. His aunt unpacked a bag of tangerines and set them out in a fan, because Grandfather had eaten tangerines every winter of his life, peeling them in one unbroken ribbon and dropping the peel into his shirt pocket like a man saving it for later.

Jackson had brought his own offering, and it was the wrong one, and he knew it was the wrong one before he even took it out of his backpack. A bottle of hot sauce, the ghost pepper kind he and his grandfather had dared each other over two summers ago, the kind that had catalyzed a whole evening of gasping and milk-drinking and laughing until his grandfather had to sit down on the porch step. He had thought of it in the car and been proud of it. Now, next to the tangerines and the photograph and the crossed marillas of orange flowers, it looked like a joke at a funeral.

"No," he said out loud, mostly to himself, and put the bottle back in the bag.

His aunt noticed. She was the one in the family who kept the calendar of obligations, who knew whose birthday fell on which saint's day, who could recite the chronology of every divorce and reconciliation without malice. She looked at the backpack, then at his face, and did not ask what was in it. Instead she picked up a marigold from the pile of stems and held it out.

"You know why these, mijo?" she asked. "The color and the smell. They guide the souls home. That's what my mother told me, for the first and second of November, when the dead come back." She was not lecturing; she was handing him a flower while she said it, already turning back to straighten the photograph so that his grandfather's eyes faced the room. "You have to make a path."

Jackson knelt and began laying the stems. His mother wanted them in a vase; his aunt wanted them scattered from the door to the table, so the scent would lead someone in. He did both, a small cluster at the base of the ofrenda and then a loose line of petals across the floor, unsure which version his grandfather would have found less ridiculous. Probably he would have found both ridiculous, and then he would have eaten a tangerine and stayed anyway, because he had never once left a room his wife had decorated while she was still standing in it.

Later, when the hall had filled and a small band was tuning guitars near the stage, Jackson took the hot sauce bottle back out. He set it beside the tangerines, cap off, the way you'd leave a drink for someone expected. A girl about his age stopped at their table, looked at the photograph, looked at the bottle, and smiled like she understood something. He didn't ask her what. He was still working out what he himself understood, whether he believed any of it literally, whether belief was even the right instrument for a task like this, or whether laying a scented path for a dead man was simply a way of saying that the dead man was still, in some stubborn accounting, owed a place to arrive. His grandfather would have called the whole thing very epicurean, all this food left out for people who couldn't eat it, and then he would have taken a tangerine from the altar and eaten it himself, right there, winking.

The band started playing. Jackson's mother reached over and turned the photograph a quarter inch, toward the marigolds, toward the door.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
story:
Hunter got the job on a Tuesday, at Ray's Family Market, four blocks from his house. Mr. Kessler, the owner, wrote $7.25 on a yellow sticky note and slid it across the counter. "That's starting pay," he said. "Bagging, carts, stock on Sundays. You can start Thursday." Hunter said thank you and put the note in his pocket. It stayed there through dinner, through the dishes, through the game he half-watched with his father, who only said, "A job's a job," when Hunter mentioned the number.

Dez lived two streets over and had also just gotten a job, at a supermarket in Fairmont, across the river. Fairmont was in a different state, twenty minutes by bridge, and Dez's cousin worked there and had gotten him in. On Saturday they sat on the tailgate of Dez's brother's truck in the driveway, phones out, comparing their first paychecks on the banking app.

"Twelve ten," Dez said, turning his screen around.

Hunter looked at his own deposit. Seven twenty-five times twenty-six hours. He did it twice, as though the app might have dropped something. "Same job," he said. "Same everything. You bag, I bag."

"Welcome to Fairmont," Dez said, grinning, but Hunter wasn't grinning, and after a minute Dez wasn't either.

They argued about it the way they argued about everything, which meant they didn't. Dez said the answer was obvious: cross the bridge, apply at his store, stop working for a man paying 2009 prices. Hunter said his mother knew Mr. Kessler, and the store was four blocks away, and he didn't have a car. Dez said his brother could drive him. Hunter said his brother already did enough driving him places. The argument reached the detente their arguments always reached, both of them on the tailgate, neither moving, and then Dez's brother came out and told them to quit sitting on his truck.

That night Hunter looked it up himself. He had planned to ask his economics teacher, but school was out, and anyway he didn't like asking people things when he could find them. He found a government page, plain white, small text, and read it twice to be sure. "The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009," he said out loud, alone in his room, to hear it in a voice. Below that, the page said many states and cities set a higher minimum. He clicked the map. His state was gray, the federal number. Across the river, Fairmont's state was a darker shade.

He sat with that for a while. The bridge was twenty minutes. His mother had gotten him the interview at Ray's by mentioning his name to Mr. Kessler at church, and she'd been pleased in a quiet way he didn't want to undo. But twenty-six hours at $7.25 was $188.50, and the same twenty-six hours across the river was $314.60, and he was trying to save for books in the fall, the fall being college, which was now eight weeks away and costing more every time he thought about it.

He thought about Mr. Kessler, too, who was saturnine at the register but had once driven Hunter's mother home when her car wouldn't start, and who presumably hadn't raised the wage because, as far as Hunter could tell, he didn't have to. Hunter tried to hold both of these at once: that Kessler was decent in the ways he was decent, and that decency and the number on the sticky note were separate things. He couldn't get them to fit together cleanly, and he decided that might be fine.

On Sunday, Hunter bagged groceries for four hours. Around noon a woman came through with two small kids and WIC checks, and the register rejected one of the items, a specific cereal, and she stood there while Kessler voided things and the line built behind her. She didn't beseech anyone, didn't explain herself, just swapped the box for the right one and kept her eyes on the belt. Hunter bagged the new box. He'd been there four hours and his feet already hurt, and he kept doing the math in his head anyway, multiplying the ache by the hours by the rate.

At the end of his shift, he asked Kessler if he could talk to him for a second. Kessler came out from behind the register, arms folded, waiting, and Hunter said he'd gotten another offer across the river and wanted to know if there was any room on the rate. Kessler looked at him for a long moment, then at the schedule taped by the time clock.

"You start college in the fall," Kessler said. It wasn't a question. "You'll leave anyway."

"August eighteenth," Hunter said.

Kessler unfolded his arms and rubbed his jaw. "I can do eight. That's what I can do." He said it flatly, like a price on a receipt, and Hunter understood it was the ceiling and that there was no ceremony attached to it. He also understood, standing there, that eight was not twelve-ten, and that a man across a bridge he'd never crossed was willing to pay him five dollars more an hour for the same work, and that neither of those facts made Kessler a liar, exactly.

He said he'd think about it, and walked home in the heat with the sun going down behind Ray's sign. When he got to the driveway, Dez was sitting on the front steps of Hunter's house, phone in hand, screen already loaded to the Fairmont supermarket's application page, turned toward the street like an offering. "You can put my cousin down as a referral," Dez said. "Line three."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Kahlo painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera; they remarried the following year.
story:
Jessica spread the print across the picnic table and pinned its corners with rocks from her mother's garden border. The Two Fridas looked up at her, two women seated hand in hand on a bench, one in a white European dress, one in a Tehuana dress the color of deep water. Her assignment sheet, folded twice in her back pocket, asked for a formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism, and it forbade biography, a rule she'd already read four times because it seemed to want something from her she couldn't yet name.

Her neighbor Marcus came through the gap in the fence without knocking, which was the arrangement between their houses. He carried a battered shoebox of seed packets, because what Marcus wanted that summer was a cutting garden along the fence line, dahlias and zinnias, something he could photograph and sell at the farmers market by August. He set the box down at the far end of the table, out of the painting's light, and asked what she was doing.

"Learning to critique a painting before Tuesday," Jessica said. "I have to talk about it for ten minutes and I've never done this before." She pointed at the two figures. "There's a heart in each of them, and the European one has cut a vein with surgical scissors, and the blood spills onto her white skirt in these deliberate red drops. I can describe that. What I can't do is say what it means without just telling the class a story about her life, and we're not allowed to lean on biography."

Marcus leaned over the print, careful of the rocks. He was quieter than usual, and Jessica suspected the seed money was thinner than he'd admitted, but she didn't ask. Instead she made herself begin the exercise her teacher had suggested, naming what she actually saw. The left Frida sat slightly forward, the right Frida slightly back, and the stormy sky behind them was divided, she noticed, by nothing at all; the horizon line cut across both women equally, holding them in one field of paint. The two hearts were joined by a thin red thread, held at its midpoint by the small Frida's hand.

"So the composition says they're one person," she said slowly, "even while the colour says they're opposites. Warm side, cold side. But the thread is the same red as the blood, so the connection is also the wound." Marcus said that was the kind of sentence you could photograph, meaning it as a compliment, and she wrote it down.

Then he tapped the bottom corner of the print. "What's this number?" Beside a name she couldn't pronounce and a museum she'd never visited, the small caption read 1939. Jessica turned to her laptop, which she'd carried out on a cutting board like a tray, and looked up the date properly, because until that moment she had been treating the painting as timeless, a self-portrait of a divided self floating outside history. What she found stopped her with her hand still on the trackpad. Kahlo had painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera, and they had remarried the following year.

"That changes the blood," Jessica said. "I was going to call it a painting about being two people, and I still think it is, but it's also about a specific year. The cut vein, the storm, the white dress like a wedding dress that's also a shroud. She painted the wound while it was open, and then a year later she went back." She heard how it sounded and corrected herself. "I don't know that she went back because of the painting. I only know the dates. I have to be careful not to build a story the paint doesn't support."

Marcus had begun sorting his seed packets into rows while she talked, and now he interposed a jalapeno envelope between two flower packets with a faint frown. "I like it better your first way," he said, a little querulous, the way he got when his grandfather criticized the garden plan. "Just two selves, one heart. The date stuff makes it about a man." Jessica considered that. It was a fair objection. She had spent an hour on the formal analysis precisely to avoid reducing the work to gossip, and now the date threatened to drag Diego into every drop of red paint.

"That's the thing, though," she said. "It can be both. The formal stuff, the split composition, the colour opposition, the thread, that's how she made the feeling visible. The date tells me the feeling had a history, that it wasn't some abstract condition she invented for the canvas. If I only do the first part it's solipsism, like the painting exists in a sealed room. If I only do the second part I'm just reading her diary out loud." She pulled the assignment sheet from her pocket and smoothed it flat beside the print. "Maybe the rule against biography is really a rule against using biography instead of looking. Maybe I can use it after I've looked."

Marcus shrugged, satisfied or at least willing to be, and went to fill the watering can. Jessica sat down on the bench beside the table and read her own notes over once, then crossed out the sentence about opposites and rewrote it in the margin in small letters: the colour divides them, the thread insists they are one. She looked up at the actual sky over the actual fence, which was clear and ordinary and going gold at the edge, and then back down at the painted one, still stormy after all these years, and she left both sentences where they were. Behind her, water hissed into the dry soil by the fence, and Marcus called out, "If these come up, you get the first bloom."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
story:
The registration page asked for her date of birth before it asked for anything else, which Kaylee decided was either sensible or insulting, depending on how she felt about being reduced to three numbers before being asked her name. She typed it in anyway. February 14, 2007. "Valentine's baby," her grandmother liked to announce to strangers, as though it were a credential.

"You're actually doing it," her brother Danny said from the doorway, holding a bowl of cereal he had clearly resuscitated from some earlier hour, the milk gone grey at the edges.

"I'm registering. It's not the vote yet." She kept her eyes on the screen. "The vote is in October."

"Same thing." He leaned over her shoulder, breathing cereal fumes onto the keyboard. "Who are you voting for?"

"I don't know. That's the entire point of registering now, so I have time to figure it out." She angled her body between him and the monitor, a move she had perfected around age nine and never abandoned.

When the confirmation screen appeared, it informed her that her voter information card would arrive by mail, and beneath that, in small print, it welcomed her as one of Canada's newest electors. She sat back. Something about the phrase got her. Newest electors, plural, as though a whole cohort of people born in early 2007 were arriving at the same door at the same moment, all of them eighteen and none of them sure of anything.

She texted her grandfather, who answered everything, usually at length. Do you know how long 18 year olds could vote in Canada? His reply came in pieces: a thumbs up, then "since 1970," then "before that you had to be 21," then a voice memo she didn't open. Fifty-five years, she thought. Her mother had been born in 1972, into a country where an eighteen-year-old could vote but where most eighteen-year-olds apparently didn't, or didn't in the numbers that made anyone nervous. Kaylee tried to imagine her grandfather at twenty, ineligible, reading about an election he couldn't touch. She couldn't picture him young. She could barely picture him without a lawn to complain about.

At dinner, her mother asked how the registration had gone, and Kaylee mentioned the 1970 thing, and Danny, predictably, said, "That's it? That's basically yesterday."

"That's before Mom was born," Kaylee said.

"Basically yesterday," Danny said again, with the authority of someone who had recently learned that history existed.

"1970," her mother said, tasting the year. "People my age were the first babies of it. The first eighteen-year-olds who could vote." She passed the potatoes. "My father says he voted for the first time in 1972 and it was the most important thing he ever did, and also that he can't remember who he voted for, which I find very honest."

Later, alone in her room, Kaylee made a list. Not of candidates, but of what she actually wanted, which kept sliding sideways into what she thought she should want, and what her grandfather wanted, and what a viral post had wanted earlier that week before fact-checkers dismantled it for what her civics teacher would have called, with evident relish, chicanery. The post had claimed a candidate had said something she demonstrably hadn't; the correction reached one-tenth as many people. Kaylee had almost believed it for an afternoon. She wasn't proud of the afternoon.

Her grandfather's voice memo, when she finally played it, was four minutes long and mostly tangential, involving a story about a snowstorm and a polling station in a church basement, and then, near the end, his voice dropped into the register he used for things that mattered. "The vote isn't a verdict on who you are," he said. "It's just the entry fee. You pay it so you're inside the room where the arguing happens." Kaylee played it twice, then opened her notes app and wrote inside the room, which she suspected she would misinterpret later, the way she was already misinterpreting half of what she'd ever been told.

In October, the card came in the mail, her name printed in a font that seemed designed to inspire confidence in institutions. She carried it to the kitchen table, where Danny grabbed it and held it up like a trophy. "One vote," he said. "Gonna cancel out exactly one annoying person somewhere. Statistically, probably a guy named Gary."

"It doesn't work like that," Kaylee said.

"It absolutely works like that. Ask Gary."

She took the card back and set it on the counter, squared with the edge, where it stayed all week, face up, her name and her polling station and the date, saying nothing definitive about anything. On election night she would sit right here with her laptop open, but that was a problem for a future Kaylee. For now she opened the fridge, considered the leftovers, and called out, "Danny, is this soup still good or are we going to resuscitate it?"

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Deliberate practice means working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, which improves skill more than simply playing through pieces already known.
story:
The garage smelled of cut grass and the cold metal of his father's old workbench, and Joseph sat on an upturned milk crate with his grandmother's guitar across his knees, playing the opening of "Wish You Were Here" for the ninth time that afternoon. He had it clean now. Every note landed where he aimed it, and the familiar chords rolled out warm and easy, and he was about to start it a tenth time when his sister Priya came through the side door carrying her violin case and a bag of chips she was clearly not intending to share.

"You're playing the same thing again," she said, settling onto the porch cooler they'd dragged in years ago and never returned. "I could hear it through the wall. Twice. Maybe more."

"It sounds good."

"It did sound good. The first six times." She opened the chips, extruding one from the bag with the careful fingers of someone rationing a limited supply, and pointed it at the sheet music leaning against the paint cans. "What's that thing you keep skipping?"

He followed her finger. Two bars, mid-page, where the tablature turned into a stretch his left hand simply could not make. He'd been flipping past them for two weeks, the way you drive around a blocked street, and he had developed a quiet taxonomy of excuses: his hands were small, the guitar had high action, the song was better without that section anyway. He said none of this. He played the two bars, and they collapsed, strings buzzing, the fourth fret abandoned somewhere in the middle of the reach.

Priya winced on his behalf, which was somehow worse than laughing. "My teacher did that to me Tuesday," she said. "I played the first page of my piece and she stopped me before I even got to finish it. She said playing through what you already know feels great and teaches you nothing, and then she assigned me four measures. Four. Out of three pages."

"That's brutal."

"It's called deliberate practice," Priya said, and stole a chip. "You work on the specific thing you're bad at, with a goal, and she's sitting right there telling me the instant I get it wrong. I hated every minute of it. Also I got those four measures better in one day than the rest of the piece got in a month." She brushed salt off her skirt, circumspect, deciding whether to say the next part. "I want to play the whole piece at the spring recital. The actual whole thing. If I keep only replaying the part I love, I'll stand up there and play thirty beautiful seconds and then die."

Joseph looked at the two bars again. Somewhere in the back of his mind he had known, for two weeks, exactly what he was doing, and it stung a little that it took his little sister eating chips in a garage to make the knowledge loud. He set a goal, since Priya's teacher apparently demanded one: the stretch, clean, five times in a row. He didn't have a teacher, so he made Priya the feedback. "Count my attempts," he said. "Tell me when it's wrong. Don't be nice."

"I'm never nice," she said, and put the chips down, which for her was an act of real sacrifice.

He played the two bars slowly, wrong. She said "one, wrong" in the flat voice of a lifeguard. He adjusted his thumb behind the neck, curled his fingers, tried again; a buzz on the fourth string, "two, wrong." The sixth attempt rang clear, and she said "one" in the counting-good voice, and he felt something absurdly bright open in his chest. On the third clean repetition his hand cramped and he had to shake it out, and Priya slid the chip bag across the floor to him without being asked, because she had been watching his face go white with concentration and knew what that cost.

They worked like that for forty minutes, her calling attempts, him failing the fifth clean repetition twice and starting the count over while the light through the garage door went from yellow to amber. When he finally got five in a row, she applauded by slapping the cooler lid, and he played the whole passage from the top, and this time the blocked street opened and the melody walked straight through.

"It still needs speed," he said, listening to himself.

"It needs a lot of things," Priya said. "You're going to have to do that whole ugly business again tomorrow, and the day after, and probably for weeks. I don't know if I'll be free to count every time."

He nodded. He didn't know either; that was the part nobody had a method for. But he propped the sheet music open to the page anyway, weighted it with a wrench so morning-Joseph couldn't turn past it, and Priya picked her violin back up and played her four measures into the rafters, slow and deliberate and already better than Tuesday.

"One more time," she said.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: In October 2024 the Los Angeles Times did not endorse a presidential candidate after its owner blocked the editorial board's plans, and several board members resigned in protest.
story:
The note from Principal Vaughn waited in David's inbox like a splinter he could not stop touching. He had opened it four times during sixth period, and now, in the library's back corner where the newspaper staff kept two mismatched desks, he opened it a fifth time. The Clarion had planned an editorial endorsing Marcus Oyelaran for student council president on a platform of reallocating the activities fund, which happened to be the fund that paid for the Principal's annual leadership retreat. "I'd ask you to reconsider running that piece," Vaughn had written, insouciant enough to add a smiley face, as though reconsideration were a small favor between friends.

David printed the editorial anyway and left it in the tray, then walked to the circulation desk to clear his head. Behind the counter, Ms. Ferreira was stamping returns, and he asked, almost idly, whether the library kept the Los Angeles Times on microfilm or if he needed the databases. "Databases," she said, not looking up. "You looking for something?" He said maybe. He didn't say that a senior named Priya had mentioned something in the newsroom two weeks ago, half-gossip, half-warning: that even the big papers had owners, and owners sometimes said no.

He found it in fifteen minutes. In October 2024, the Los Angeles Times had not endorsed a presidential candidate. That part he learned first, from the archived editorial page, a strange blank where a recommendation should have been. Then, piecing together the reporting that followed, he learned the rest: the paper's owner had blocked the editorial board's plans, and the paper's own journalists wrote about it openly. Several members of the editorial board resigned in protest. He sat back in the chair with its cracked vinyl armrests and read the names of the people who had quit. Ordinary names. People who had decided that a blank page was worse than no job.

Priya found him there, dropped her backpack on the table. "Vaughn got to you too?" she said. He showed her the principal's email, and she made a sound between a laugh and something harder. "So what are you going to do, run it and get shut down, or fold like cheap laundry?" David turned the monitor toward her. "Read this," he said. She read, and her face changed the way faces do when a small local problem turns out to have ancestors.

They argued about it until the library closed at eight. Priya's position was simple: print the endorsement, make Vaughn censor them in writing, and thereby prove the point more loudly than any editorial could. David kept coming back to the resignations. "Those people quit," he said, "and the paper still ran, and the owner still owned it. They didn't win. They just refused to pretend." Priya said refusing wasn't nothing. He wasn't sure. He had been editor for a year and had inured himself to small compromises, the softened headline, the quote cut to spare a teacher's feelings, each one defensible, each one making the next easier. Somewhere in that accumulation, he thought, a paper stops being a paper, though he could not say exactly when the change happened, which bothered him more than the principal did.

The solution he arrived at was uglier and more honest than either of their positions. On Thursday the Clarion ran its election issue with the endorsement of Marcus exactly as drafted, but above it, on the same page, an editor's note, unsigned because David had insisted it be his byline alone: "An administrator asked us to reconsider this editorial. We are printing it, and printing the fact that we were asked not to." He knew the note was itself a kind of leverage, a move in a game he claimed to stand apart from, and he let that contradiction sit in him unresolved rather than paper over it.

Vaughn summoned him Friday morning. The office was warm and smelled of coffee, and the principal did not shout. He called the editor's note "unfortunate framing," and David recognized the maneuver, the careful dysphemism, an endorsement becoming "that piece," a threat becoming a request, a censor becoming a concerned administrator. "You know I fund that paper," Vaughn said, mild as milk. "I know," David said. "It's in the budget." Neither of them mentioned the retreat. The silence stretched until Vaughn waved him out, which David understood was not a victory, only a postponement.

He walked back through the hall past the trophy case, and in the glass he could see the library doors at the far end, the place where he had found, in a fifty-year-old paper's small collapse, both a warning and a permission. He still didn't know whether the board members who resigned had done the right thing or merely the clean thing, whether quitting was courage or abandonment, and he suspected he would not know until he stood where they had stood. For now the paper was out, Marcus's name in bold, the note beneath it, and Priya was taping a copy of the page to the newsroom door as he came in. "There's your blank page," she said. "Full."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
story:
The morning smelled of wet asphalt and coffee, and Alexander carried both into the community hall like contraband. He was eighteen years and twenty-three days old, and this was his first federal election, a fact he had mentioned to his grandmother so many times in the last month that she had started answering the phone with "Yes, Alexander, I know, you're voting." She had died in March. Since then nobody eulogized her better than Alexander himself did, quietly, on walks, in the shower, composing sentences he would never say out loud. He had promised her this vote the way other people promise their grandparents graduation photos.

The hall had been a badminton court in some earlier life; the lines were still visible under the folding tables, and volunteers in laminated lanyards moved along them like players in a slow rally. Alexander joined the short line and rehearsed what he would say. His father's voice was in one ear, his civics seminar in the other. His father, who had voted the same way for thirty years and called it chess, believed a vote was a tool, something you aimed at the least bad outcome. His teacher, Ms. Okonjo, believed a vote was a statement, a small public philosophy. Alexander had spent the election period unable to decide whether he was a chess player or a philosopher, and this morning the question had a deadline.

"Name," said the woman at the table. Her badge said DIANE. She had a pen behind each ear, which Alexander found quietly wonderful.

"Alexander Petrou. Uh, this is my first time." He handed over his driver's licence with the self-consciousness of a man presenting a passport at a border he wasn't sure he had the right to cross.

Diane typed, frowned, typed again. "You're not on the voters list."

The floor seemed to tilt toward him. He had assumed the list was like a class roster, something the world kept for you automatically. "I never got anything in the mail," he said. "I moved for school in September. I figured I was, I don't know, in the system."

"Are you still resident here? In this riding?"

"Yes. My parents' address. I'm home this weekend." He had come home specifically to vote, had argued with himself about which ballot he belonged on, and now it appeared he belonged on none.

"Then you can register here, today," Diane said. "At your assigned polling place. Just need ID with that address, or a piece of mail and something with your name on it."

Alexander stared at her. He had spent three weeks certain that forgetting to register meant forfeiting the whole thing, that democracy had a paperwork wall and he had walked into it face first. The discovery sat in him strangely, half relief and half embarrassment at his own certainty. How many other walls had he imagined? He caught himself wondering, with genuine curiosity, what else he believed wrongly about how the country worked, and whether everyone carried around a private, inaccurate epistemology like a second wallet.

He emptied his pockets onto the table: licence, a bank card, a crumpled hydro bill from his father's stack at home. Diane flattened the bill with the heel of her hand. "This works." She wrote his name onto a form, printed a voter registration certificate, and directed him to table four, where another volunteer crossed his name off with a satisfying stroke of purple ink. The whole thing had taken six minutes. Six minutes to be invented as a voter.

The ballot was smaller than he expected, a slip of paper the size of a receipt, as though something so consequential should weigh more. Behind the cardboard screen, he read the names top to bottom twice. His father's candidate was third, his teacher's was first, and between them sat the question he had carried since March. What was a vote for, exactly? A lever, or a sentence about who you were? He noticed that his hand was hovering and that he was smiling at his own hand, this absurd, trembling machine that had to decide alone now that both his advisors were gone. His grandmother would have told him to stop thinking and mark something. She had also, once, driven an hour to deliver a winter coat to an indigent man she'd read about in the paper, without ever voting differently from her husband, so the two of them had cancelled each other out for forty years, and she had seemed fine with that arithmetic.

He marked the ballot. He would not tell his father which box, and he would tell Ms. Okonjo only that he had voted, and he still did not know whether he had played chess or written a sentence, and he suspected he would not know for years, maybe not ever, maybe the not-knowing was the actual adult condition that everyone had been too polite to mention. The pencil had no eraser, which struck him as either an oversight or a philosophy.

He fed the ballot into the box, listened to the soft click of it landing among the others, and stood for a moment with his empty hands. Outside, the rain had stopped. A man at the next table was arguing cheerfully with a volunteer about the polling place assignment, waving a letter, and the volunteer was saying, gently, "You can sort it out right here today."

Alexander took one of the pencils from the little cup by the door. Nobody stopped him.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In periodized training, a season is divided into cycles; a microcycle, the smallest, usually lasts about one week.
story:
The gym smelled like rubber and cold concrete, and Laurence had the clipboard against her knees because the bleachers were too high to write on. Around her the junior team ran suicides, sneakers squeaking, and Coach Ferreira sat two rows down with her arms crossed, watching no one in particular. Laurence was supposed to hand her a training week by Friday. That was the deal: she wanted to be captain, and the coach had said, "Then show me you can build a week, not just survive one."

She had drafted it Sunday night at the kitchen table. Monday sprints, Tuesday weights, Wednesday sprints again, Thursday match play, Friday weights, Saturday scrimmage, Sunday more sprints, because Sunday was when everyone else slacked. She'd been proud of the density of it, the way the days pressed together like folded steel.

"That's a schedule for machines," said Priya, flopping onto the bleachers beside her after the suicides, hair stuck to her forehead. Priya had been injured in October, a hamstring that tore because nobody had warmed up properly in the rain, and she'd come back in January slower and warier. "You put me in that week and I'm done by Thursday."

"You're the fittest one we have."

"My hamstring doesn't care how fit I am." Priya pulled the clipboard toward her, scanned it, and Laurence let her, which was itself a concession. "Where's the rest?"

"Rest is for people who don't want it enough."

Priya looked at her for a long second. "You sound like an autocrat," she said, and handed the clipboard back. "Like a small one. A gym autocrat."

Laurence laughed before she could stop herself, and then didn't apologize for it, and then didn't take the line out of the plan either.

After practice she stayed behind, ostensibly to collect cones. Actually she went to the office alcove where the coach kept her binders, shelves of them, spines labeled by season. She wasn't sneaking, she told herself; she was doing research. In the binder marked with last year's dates she found week-by-week sheets, and each sheet had a word typed at the top that she'd never seen before: microcycle.

"You're in my binders," Ferreira said from the doorway. She didn't sound angry.

"What's a microcycle?"

"Come here." Ferreira pulled a sheet out, one week on a single page, hard days and easy days laid out like weather. "In periodized training, a season gets divided into cycles. The microcycle is the smallest one. It usually lasts about one week." She tapped the page. "That's what you're writing. You're not writing seven days. You're writing one unit."

Laurence looked at the sheet. There was a rest day in it, an actual blank day, and two of the days were marked "activation," which when she flipped back she found meant warm-ups counted as content, not as an apology before the real work. The week was shaped. It had a top and a slope down.

She rewrote the plan that night at the kitchen table, the same table, the same pen. Monday hard, Tuesday easy, Wednesday hardest, Thursday technical with long warm-ups, Friday moderate, Saturday scrimmage, Sunday nothing. Sunday nothing. It looked lazy. It looked like a document written by someone altruistic, someone concerned with other people's hamstrings, and she sat with her discomfort about that until she understood it wasn't discomfort about them. It was discomfort about letting go of the version of herself that believed effort meant stacking.

She also kept one thing. Monday sprints stayed, first thing, no negotiation, because she had decided she was allowed to be a little bit of a tyrant about Mondays specifically.

Friday she handed the clipboard to Ferreira in the gym, under the far basket while the juniors ran their warm-up laps. The coach read it slowly, the way she read everything, and Laurence stood with her hands behind her back and admitted to herself she could not tell from the woman's face whether this was passing or failing.

"Microcycle," Ferreira said finally.

"I found it in your binder. I hope that's okay."

"That's what binders are for." Ferreira closed the clipboard. "Captain's announced Monday."

Laurence nodded and went to set up the cones, arranging them in the pattern for the warm-up drill, and it was only halfway through the second line of cones that she registered what the coach had said. She turned around. Ferreira was already walking toward the juniors, and Priya was jogging over from the storage room with the ball bag, calling out, "Coach, who's the new captain, then?" And Ferreira pointed at Priya, without breaking stride, and said, "Her hamstring approved the week, so she's got my vote, but the team votes Monday."

Laurence stood between the cones with her hand still raised from placing one, and started laughing, and put the cone down.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
story:
Maria sat in the corner booth of the Cedar Fork with her hands folded on the table, waiting for the manager. The restaurant smelled like onions and floor cleaner. She had a folder on her lap with one page in it, a page she had rewritten three times since Tuesday. On the page was a single sentence: "Tell me about a time you handled conflict in a group."

Her brother Dev had told her interviews were rigged toward people who could talk about themselves, and that the only fair way to fight that was preparation. He'd printed something off the internet and slid it across the kitchen table. "It's called STAR," he said, chewing a piece of toast. "Situation, Task, Action, Result." He hadn't explained further; he was seventeen and believed explanations were a form of condescension. She'd read the printout herself, twice, then folded it into the folder.

The story she had chosen was the chemistry project from last spring. Priya, Marco, and a fourth kid named Elliot whom nobody had wanted, had been assigned a presentation on water treatment. Elliot had turned out to be bellicose about nearly everything: fonts, slide order, whether the word "flocculation" was too hard for the class. He'd shouted at Priya in the library until a librarian came over, and after that the group had stopped meeting together, meeting instead in pairs, in fragments, in the hallway before class.

The manager came out at four minutes past two, carrying a paper cup. She was shorter than Maria expected, with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair. "Maria? I'm Ruth. You applied for the Saturday host position." She sat down across from her, set the cup aside, and opened a small notebook. "First job?" "Yes." "That's fine. Everyone here had one." She clicked a pen. "Tell me about a time you worked with a group and something went wrong."

Maria's rehearsed sentence dissolved. What came out instead was the truth: that the project had gone wrong slowly, in the way things do, that nobody could name the day it failed. She heard herself talking about the library, about Elliot's voice, about Priya leaving the table. Ruth kept writing. Maria thought, with the clarity of panic, that she was telling this badly, in the wrong order, and then she thought about the folded page.

She put her hand flat on the folder but didn't open it. "Let me start over. There's a way to tell these, I practiced it. Situation, task, action, result." She laid it out. The situation: four students, one grade, three weeks. The task: her piece was the research, but she'd also taken on getting the group to function at all, because someone had to. The action: instead of holding a group meeting, which had already exploded once, she went to each person separately, one lunch period at a time, and asked what they needed from the others. Marco wanted Elliot to stop rewriting his slides. Priya wanted an apology, or at least an acknowledgment. Elliot, it turned out, had been sure from the start that the others were going to cut him out, and had decided to be loud before he could be quiet.

Ruth looked up. "And the result?" "We split the presentation into four solo sections so nobody touched anybody else's work. We got an A minus." Maria paused. "It wasn't really solved. It was more like an arbitration nobody agreed to. I made a ruling and they accepted it because nobody wanted another library scene. I still don't know if that was the right thing or just the thing that worked." Ruth stopped writing. She took a slow drink from the cup and studied Maria over the rim.

"You didn't put that on your application," she said. "The part about not knowing." "I didn't think it helped." "Here's what I know after eleven years of this. On Saturdays I have two servers who've filed complaints against each other twice. I've settled it twice. My way of settling it is I underwrite whatever truce they make, meaning if it falls apart on a Saturday night, it falls apart on me. I need someone at the door who can read a room before it goes loud." She closed the notebook. "Can you start this Saturday at ten?"

Maria said yes before she had finished deciding whether she meant it. Ruth stood, then stopped, hand on the back of the booth. "One thing. When you split the presentation into four parts, did the class notice it was four separate projects wearing one title?" "The teacher did," Maria said. "She wrote on the rubric, 'Functioning apart is not the same as functioning together.'" Ruth laughed once, a short sound, and pushed her glasses down onto her nose.

On her way out, Maria passed the two servers, a tall woman and a younger man, setting tables on opposite sides of the room without looking at each other. She recognized the geometry of it, the careful distances, the pairs meeting in fragments. She stopped at the door, then turned back toward the host stand, where the Saturday chart was taped with names in two different inks, and began reading it.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma.
story:
Brooklyn signed her name on the volunteer sheet at the St. Vincent food bank and noticed, beneath it, a column headed "Hours." Behind her, a boy from her school, Dev, was already filling his in.

"You've got thirty-eight written down," she said, looking over his shoulder. "I have zero."

"Deadline's Friday," Dev said. "Graduation's in June, but the school wants the paperwork in before the diploma meeting." He capped his pen. "Forty hours of community involvement, or you don't get the Ontario Secondary School Diploma. I've been putting it off since grade nine."

Brooklyn had known about the requirement for years the way she knew about the periodic table, as a fact that lived in school and never followed her home. Now it had followed her to a church basement that smelled of cardboard and dish soap, where pallets of canned corn stood against one wall and a woman named Ruth was sorting bread with quick, practiced hands.

"Brooklyn, was it?" Ruth said. "You're on the bread table. Check dates, pull anything green or furry, and don't agonize over it. The compost doesn't judge."

She worked through the morning. A man came in with his daughter, maybe four years old, and took a box of rice, two cartons of eggs, a bag of apples that had gone soft on one side. Brooklyn watched him thank Ruth twice, once at the counter and once at the door, as if the first time hadn't been enough. The girl waved at nobody in particular.

In grade ten, Brooklyn remembered, her civics teacher had asked who was volunteering and why, and a girl named Priya had said she tutored immigrant kids in math because her grandmother had been helped that way forty years ago. Another girl had said she did shoreline cleanup because it looked good on applications. The teacher had written both reasons on the board and asked the class which was better, and the class had argued until the bell, and nothing was decided. Brooklyn had said nothing. She had wanted a reason that fit entirely on one line, and she had never found one.

Today she had come, honestly, because of the deadline. Her guidance counselor had flagged her file in April: forty hours still outstanding, and Ontario high school students could not earn the diploma without them. Brooklyn had resented the errand all the way here, resenting most the possibility that she was the kind of person who only showed up when a certificate was held hostage. But by noon she had learned the bread table, and where the dated milk went, and that Ruth had volunteered here eleven years and still got the sorting bins confused on Mondays.

Dev, meanwhile, was intransigent about the scanner. A new inventory app had been installed on the food bank's single tablet, and Ruth wanted the cans logged digitally. Dev insisted the paper list was faster and refused, politely but completely, to switch over. "Two hours I have left to log," he said. "I'm not spending them learning software."

Brooklyn took the tablet herself. The app turned out to be simple, three taps per item, and within twenty minutes she had catalogued a shelf that would have taken Dev an hour by hand. Her arriving late and under compulsion had, in a small way, catalyzed the change; she had no loyalty to the old system, no stake in being right.

"You didn't have to do that," Dev said, watching her.

"I know. It was faster, that's all."

But driving the whole thing home, later, was a confusion she couldn't sort: whether the mandatory hours corrupted the giving or simply got people through the door who would never otherwise have come. The boy at the counter with his daughter didn't know or care why she'd sorted his apples. The soft spot was cut away either way.

Ruth called a lunch break at twelve thirty and put out sandwiches for the volunteers. She sat down across from Brooklyn and peeled an orange in one long spiral, the kind of thing a person learns from doing it ten thousand times.

"Why'd you start so late?" Ruth asked. "Most kids your age bank their hours in grade nine."

"Honestly? It was something I had to do for the diploma. Forty hours, or no graduation." Brooklyn pulled the crust off her sandwich. "That's the whole reason I'm here. I keep thinking that makes it not count."

Ruth considered this while she chewed. "Some people who start for the paper stay for the work. Some who start noble quit in a month. The reason you walked in is the least interesting thing about you by the time you walk out." She pushed half the orange across the table.

Brooklyn took it. She didn't know yet, she admitted to herself, which kind she would turn out to be, and there was no way to find out except to keep coming back after the form was signed. Two hours remained on her sheet. After that, the counting stopped and she would learn what she did when nothing was being measured.

At the end of the shift she wrote "2" in the hours column, capped Dev's pen, and looked up at Ruth sorting bread for the afternoon crowd.

"Same time next Saturday?" she said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion, but a 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo found a statistical flaw and evidence of streak shooting.
story:
The Herreraons' basement smelled like salsa and radiator dust, and by halftime Payton had claimed the corner of the couch closest to the mini-fridge, because that was where the good seat was and because Mrs. Herreron kept drifting past it, and Payton had noticed she was looking for a place to sit down.

"Jax is on fire," Derek said from the floor, pointing his pizza crust at the screen. "Eight straight points. You don't guard a man like that. You pray."

"He's not on fire," said Marcus, Derek's older brother, home from his first semester of college and apparently determined to prove it. "The hot hand is an illusion. There's a famous study. Nineteen eighty-five. Gilovich, Vallone, and Tversky. They looked at the streaks and found nothing."

"They found the Sixers," Derek said.

"They found that a made shot doesn't make the next one more likely. It's coin flips. People see patterns that aren't there."

Payton had been quiet through most of this, half watching the game and half watching Mrs. Herreron finally settle into the folding chair Derek had dragged over for her without saying anything about it. But the argument snagged on something. Her statistics teacher had made them read a paper in October, one of those things she'd assumed she'd forget, except that she hadn't, and now it was surfacing the way a name surfaces at the second introduction.

"That study's been challenged," she said.

Both brothers turned. On the screen, Jax rose for a three and missed, and Derek groaned as though she'd personally knocked the ball away.

"Challenged how?" Marcus said.

"Two thousand eighteen. Miller and Sanjurjo. They reanalyzed it." She was reaching now, pulling it up out of memory, and she was aware of the risk of reaching wrong in front of a room. "They found a flaw in the statistics. A statistical flaw. And they found evidence of streak shooting. Actual streaks."
