"So which is it?" Derek demanded. "Fire or no fire?"

"I didn't say it was one or the other."

"You said the hot hand was real."

"I said the study was flawed." Payton felt her face warm, and she also noticed that Mrs. Herreron had leaned forward, interested, her paper cup of cider held in both hands. That was worth more than winning. Still, she didn't back off. "Gilovich, Vallone, and Tversky called the hot hand an illusion, and for thirty years everybody believed them. Then somebody checked the math again."

Marcus had his phone out. "Miller and Sanjurjo," he read, half to himself. Payton watched his expression move from dismissal to something more careful, the way a person checks a price and finds it lower than expected. "Huh."

"Huh what?" Derek said.

"Huh, she's right."

"You're just saying that because she's the only one here who can do your homework."

"I'm saying it because I'm reading it." Marcus turned the screen toward Derek, and Derek squinted at it with the concentration of a man being asked to translate a language he'd only ever spoken.

The game came back from a timeout. Mr. Herreron appeared at the top of the stairs with a second tray of wings, having clearly decided the first tray had been expropriated by the teenagers before it ever reached the table, and Derek intercepted it at the bottom step with an apology that was mostly chewing.

"Bring those here," Mrs. Herreron said, patting the arm of her chair, and Derek brought them, and Payton moved her feet so the tray could rest between them.

"This is a hedonistic spread," Marcus announced, surveying the wings, the queso, the seven-layer dip going cold at the edges.

"It's the playoffs," his father said, as if that explained a philosophy of life, which in this house it did.

In the third quarter Jax scored six straight again, and the basement erupted, and Derek pointed at Payton across the chaos of standing bodies. "Hot hand. Say it. Say I'm right."

"I can't say that," she called back over the noise. But she was grinning, and she stood up too, because Jax was pulling up from the corner and there was no sitting through this. "The 2018 paper found evidence of streak shooting. That's all I can give you."

"That's everything!"

"It's not everything. The first study still exists. They're both sitting there. I don't get to pick one just because it's loud in here."

Derek laughed at that, a real laugh, and even Marcus cracked, and Mrs. Herreron reached up and tugged the hem of Payton's sleeve without saying anything, just once, the way you'd touch a sleeve to say stay.

Jax missed the next two shots and hit the one after. Derek threw his hands up as though the universe were mocking him personally. Marcus held up his phone again, as if it were a ruling. Payton sat back down between the wings and the woman who wanted them, and watched the fourth quarter decide nothing yet, all of it still possible, the scoreboard holding both arguments open at once.

"Next commercial," she said, "somebody's getting my numbers."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area between two curves is found by integrating the upper function minus the lower function over the interval where they are ordered that way.
story:
The bell over the door of Kessler's Corner Store rang twice before Nicholas noticed it, once for the woman buying lottery tickets and once for nobody, just the wind. He had spread his homework across two bags of sunflower seeds near the register end of the counter, where Mr. Kessler let him sit on weeknights, and he was staring at a graph he had drawn for the fourth time.

The problem was from math club. Yesterday, in Room 214, Priya and Marcus had squared off over the area trapped between a line and a parabola, and their answers had come out different, and different not by a sign flip but by some stranger wrongness, as though two shapes had been measured and one of them belonged to a different problem entirely. Ms. Okafor, whom the whole club half-ironically lionized, had refused to settle it. "Figure out who's wrong and why," she had said, and left early for a department meeting, and the club had dissolved into argument and then into the hallway.

Nicholas worked Saturdays here, sweeping and restocking, and tonight he had stayed past closing to think, because at home there was only the apartment's noise and here there was the refrigerator's hum and the glossy poster by the ice cream case, a nature scene of a river winding through forest, captioned with words like riparian and biome, which the store's supplier had printed to make the store look wholesome. He looked at the poster now the way he looked at the graph. A river had banks. The water lay between an upper bank and a lower one. If you wanted to know how much water, you did not measure the banks separately and add them up.

He wrote the line's equation above the parabola's on his paper. Between the two crossing points, the line sat on top; the parabola curled beneath it like a cupped hand. Priya, he remembered, had integrated the parabola minus the line, because she liked reading her equations left to right in the order they'd been printed in the problem. Marcus had done the reverse. On the interval between the crossings, one function was upper and one was lower, and the area was the integral of the upper function minus the lower function, taken across that whole stretch. Nicholas said it to himself in almost those words, quietly, and Mr. Kessler, locking the cigarette cabinet, glanced over.

"Talking to yourself now."

"Finding area," Nicholas said. "Between curves. You take the top one minus the bottom one over the whole stretch between where they cross. Priya flipped it."

"So she's wrong."

"She's wrong," Nicholas said, but he slowed on it, because Priya was not wrong the way a person is wrong about a fact. She was wrong the way a person is wrong about a direction, and directions could be stood in. He remembered her face when the numbers disagreed, the flat refusal to be embarrassed, the way she had said "one of us measured something real and one of us didn't." He had admired that more than Marcus's quick answer, which had been right and smug at once. Marcus had computed first and thought second, and Priya had thought first and computed into a mirror.

The bell rang again. Nicholas looked up and Priya herself came in, still in her track warmups, hair wet from the gym, hunting the fridge for the lime soda she liked. She saw his papers fanned across the counter and came over without asking.

"Please tell me you solved it," she said. "It kept me up."

"The line is above the parabola between the crossings," Nicholas said. "So the area is the upper minus the lower, integrated over that interval. You did it the other way around. You didn't get a different shape. You got the same shape counted as if the ground were the ceiling."

Priya pulled the paper toward her and read his work, chewing the inside of her cheek. "Same two curves," she said. "Same crossings. And Marcus just happened to write his in the right order."

"He got the right number. But he couldn't say why the order mattered. He just said 'top minus bottom' like it was a rule someone told him."

"And you can?"

Nicholas looked at the poster by the ice cream case, the river lying between its two banks, filling exactly the space the land allowed. "I think so," he said. "But I want to check the case where the curves cross in the middle of the interval, because then which one is upper switches partway through, and I don't know yet whether you split it into pieces or something else happens. That part I haven't got."

Priya sat down on the stool Mr. Kessler kept for slow afternoons and uncapped her soda. "So you're saying Marcus is right and also can't be trusted, and I'm wrong and also kind of right."

"I'm saying the top minus the bottom is what's true, and everything else is us arguing about who deserves credit for a river," Nicholas said, and nodded at the poster. Priya looked at it, laughed once, and pulled a fresh sheet of paper out of his binder.

"Draw the switching case," she said. "I'll do the algebra."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
story:
Tristan had been sitting at the corner table of the coffee shop for two hours with one cold flat white and a laptop open to the UCAS application. Six courses sat in his list. The system allowed only five. He had read the page four times, hoping the number would change, and it had not.

Nadia slid into the seat across from him, uninvited, carrying a green tea she barely touched. She had her own list folded into the pocket of her denim jacket, and she pulled it out and flattened it against the table so he could see that hers had five lines, five course codes, no hesitation.

"How did you cut yours?" he asked.

"I didn't cut anything. I never had a sixth." She tapped his screen. "Five courses maximum. That's the whole allowance. And it doesn't rank them, you know. The list is unordered. No order of preference. They just sit there, all equal."

"So the sixth one is just gone?"

"The sixth one never existed, officially." She said it lightly, but she watched his face while she said it.

The sixth course was mathematics at a university three hundred miles north. The other five were all within an hour of his mother's flat: two economics, one statistics, one joint honours, one engineering with a foundation year. He had built the list the way you build a wall, each choice braced against the others so nothing could fall. He wanted to subsume the whole decision under a single principle, and the principle he had chosen was proximity. His mother's shifts had been cut in October. Nobody had said out loud what that meant for the spring, and nobody needed to.

"I could drop the foundation year one," he said. "The engineering. That's the weakest."

"You said it was the safety."

"Safe and weak aren't opposites."

"Fine. Drop the one far away, then." Nadia said it while looking at the window, at a man struggling with an umbrella that had turned inside out. She had wanted him to apply north since September, and she had never once said so directly, which was its own kind of statement. Anxiety about choices was endemic this term; half their year had it, teachers kept saying so in assemblies. But hers ran quieter than most, and it surfaced mainly as opinions about other people's decisions.

"It's not that far," Tristan said. "Four hours by train."

"Then keep it."

He looked at the screen for a while. The five-course limit was not a moral test, he told himself, and yet it behaved like one, forcing a ranking onto a system that officially refused ranking. He could keep the wall of five nearby courses, or he could trade one brick for something he actually wanted and let the structure carry a gap. Both were defensible. He could not make both true at once, and no amount of reasoning would make the sixth slot appear.

He deleted the foundation year course. The list rebalanced itself, five items, four of them close and one far, all listed flat and equal, no preference shown anywhere on the page, which was either a mercy or an erasure. He pressed submit before he could reconsider, and the confirmation banner came up green.

"There," Nadia said. "Done."

"Not done. Now we wait."

"Then you can start drinking your coffee like a person." She pushed it toward him. He lifted the cup. It was cold, and he drank it anyway.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
story:
Luca turned eighteen on the fourth of October, eleven days before the registration deadline, and the envelope from the county arrived on the ninth: a mail ballot, two thick card pages, a privacy sleeve, and a return envelope with his name already printed in the window. He carried it to the desk in his room and set it beside the keyboard without opening it.

Downstairs, his mother was on the phone with her sister, her voice climbing into the register she used for politics. She had spent the autumn calling the challenger a crook, taping his face to the refrigerator with a magnet, sending Luca links at midnight with subject lines like READ THIS and SHARE. The morning the ballots came, she had said, "I hope you know what's at stake," and left the room before he could answer, which was how most of their conversations about the election ended.

He opened the envelope and read the instructions. You may not show your marked ballot to anyone. Your vote will be kept secret. He read the sentence twice, then typed into the search bar: why is the ballot secret. His fingers paused over the keys. It had not occurred to him that secrecy was a thing someone had to invent.

The results loaded. He skimmed past a page about election laws and found a history site with a picture of a wooden voting booth, and he read part of it out loud, quietly, because reading aloud helped him hold on to things. "The secret printed ballot," he read. "It's called the Australian ballot, because the Australian colonies of Tasmania and Victoria introduced it in 1856." He sat back. So there was a time before this, a time when everyone could watch you vote, when your landlord and your boss and your father could stand behind you and read your choices off a colored card. He tried to imagine his mother standing behind him right now, and did not have to try very hard.

His older sister, Nadia, knocked twice and came in without waiting, the way she always did. She was home from her first semester for the weekend, and she wanted something; he could tell from the way she leaned against the doorframe instead of sitting. "You doing it?" she asked. He said he was reading first. She picked up the privacy sleeve and turned it over in her hands. "Good. You're actually reading it. Dad voted for a school board guy once because the name sounded familiar."

"Did you know the ballot has a name?" Luca said. "It's called the Australian ballot. Tasmania and Victoria, 1856." Nadia raised her eyebrows. "You're going to be insufferable in college," she said, but she smiled when she said it, and then her face went serious again, which was the real reason she had come in. "Mom's downstairs telling Aunt Reza you're voting the right way. Like it's settled." She put the sleeve down. "I just thought you should know she's saying that."

Luca looked at the screen, at the wooden booth, at the date. He thought about the secrecy he had been reading about, the long argument it must have taken to make it law, the whole apparatus of sleeves and envelopes and unmarked folds, all of it built so that no one could ever do what his mother was doing downstairs: assuming his vote, spending it in advance on a phone call. At the same time he thought about her taped-up articles, some of which he had actually read, some of which had been fair. The challenger had taken money from a developer whose project the town had voted down; that part was true even if her acerbic posts about him made everything sound worse than the records showed. Both things were true at once. He did not have a word for that, and he did not need one.

His mother came up while Nadia was still there. She stood in the doorway with her tea and looked at the ballot pages lying flat on the desk. "You want help with the judges?" she asked. "Those races are impossible." He said he had the sample ballot open in another tab. She came closer, close enough to see the screen, and he watched her eyes move from the history site to the blank card pages to his hands. "You know," she said, "I'd feel better if I knew you weren't wasting this. People fought for this."

"People fought for the part where you don't get to know," Luca said.

She stared at him. "I'm not the enemy, Luca. Don't act like I'm the enemy just because that candidate has spent a year trying to vilify everyone who questions him." Her voice had gone quiet, which was worse than loud. Nadia slipped past her into the hall. His mother stayed a moment longer, and then she said something he had not expected, so quietly he almost missed it: "You know I've never actually missed one. Since I was twenty. My mother couldn't. It wasn't that kind of country." She picked a thread off her sleeve, an encumbrance she'd worn all day and only now noticed. "I just want to see it filled in. Not how. Just filled in."

After she went down, Luca sat for a while with his hand flat over the ballot pages. Then he picked up the pen, marked the races one by one, some the way his mother would have, some not, and slid the card into the sleeve. He carried it to the top of the stairs and held it up so it caught the light from the kitchen, and called, "It's filled in."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can.
story:
The two articles had been open on Vanessa's laptop since Tuesday, and by Thursday night they had stopped being articles and started being two people arguing across her kitchen table while she sat between them, unable to side with either. The first, from a ecology journal with a matte cover she'd found through the school database, claimed that montane bird species were shifting their ranges uphill as temperatures warmed, following the cool air they'd evolved to need. The second, published three years later by a team that had visited fewer sites but over more years, found no consistent shift at all, and suggested the first paper's pattern was an artifact of where its researchers had happened to place their survey points.

Her mother set a mug of tea down beside the keyboard, not asking, just setting it down, the way she did when she could tell a night was going long. The kitchen clock said nine-forty. Vanessa's draft, due Monday, was supposed to be a critical review, which her assignment sheet described as "a considered position on a scholarly debate," and so far her considered position was that she had typed the word "however" eleven times and deleted it eleven times.

"Still the birds?" her mother said, sitting across from her with her own mug.

"Still the birds."

She read the methods section of the first paper again, slowly, the way her junior-year English teacher had cajoled the class into reading poetry, one line at a time, resisting the urge to skim toward the conclusion. The first team had sampled forty-two ridgelines across two summers. The second team, eleven watersheds across nine years. Forty-two sites, two years. Eleven sites, nine years. She wrote both on a napkin and stared at them like they were scores from two different sports.

The problem, she realized, was that both papers could be describing the same mountains. A bird population could drift uphill in a hot year and drift back down in a wet one, and two studies watching different slices of time would each see only their own slice and swear it was the whole weather. She pushed the napkin away, then pulled it back. Somewhere, she thought, someone must have noticed this problem before her, someone with more than a napkin.

She searched the second paper's reference list for anything with the word "review" in the title, then tried "synthesis," then, on a guess, typed both authors' names together. The database returned a third paper, one neither article had cited much, published just last year. Its abstract began with a sentence she read three times: the authors had combined the results of dozens of studies on exactly this question, the upslope shift of montane species, in order to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study could.

"Wait," she said out loud.

"What?"

"Hang on." She was already skimming the methods, where the phrase appeared again in bold-faced certainty: a meta-analysis. A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question. It pooled the forty-two ridgelines and the eleven watersheds and forty other datasets besides, and what it found sat between the two papers like a referee: a small uphill shift overall, real but modest, smaller than the first paper claimed and larger than the second allowed.

She called her friend Priya, who was also writing a review, on hormones and adolescent sleep, and who answered on the second ring with her mouth clearly full of something.

"Did you find the thing where they pool all the studies?" Vanessa said.

"The what?"

"A meta-analysis. It combines the results of a bunch of studies on the same question, so it can estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can. Both of my articles are inside it. Like, statistically inside it."

Priya stopped chewing. "That exists?"

"Both of my authors are in the author list of the thing that proves them both partly wrong. It's brutal. It's beautiful."

After she hung up, she sat for a while with her hands flat on the table, the way her grandmother used to do before deciding whether bread dough had risen enough, a patience Vanessa had always read as discernment rather than delay, though she couldn't have said how she knew the difference. Her grandmother had been dead two years, and Vanessa thought, not for the first time, that the woman would have understood the napkin with the two numbers on it, the weighing of small evidence.

Because here was what the night had actually taught her, and it wasn't the answer. The meta-analysis gave an answer, a pooled slope, a confidence interval, but its own final paragraph flagged exactly the thing she'd guessed at on the napkin: study design varied, some datasets were short, some surveys were placed in ways that might bias the result. The referee was better informed than either fighter and still not omniscient. Her review, she saw now, would not be a verdict. It would be a description of how the two papers disagreed, why, and what a pooling of all the evidence so far suggested, with its edges left visible.

She opened a new document and typed the first real sentence she'd written all week: "These two studies reach opposite conclusions not because one is wrong, but because each saw part of a pattern." Then she deleted "not because one is wrong," because she wasn't sure that was true, and because she was starting to distrust sentences that settled things. She retyped it: "Each study saw part of a pattern, and only part."

Her mother came back for the empty mugs. Vanessa turned the laptop so she could see the forest of little squares on the meta-analysis's summary figure, each square a study, each horizontal line the uncertainty around it, the diamond at the bottom the pooled estimate that no single square could have drawn alone.

"That's tomorrow's you talking," her mother said, tapping the diamond.

"That's Monday's me, actually," Vanessa said, and saved the file.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
story:
Isabella found her name on the fridge before she found anyone she knew, both of them attached to the same magnet, her name in gold marker on a white poster that said CONGRATULATES OUR GRADUATES, 2022. The party was in Dev's backyard, string lights sagging between the fence and the garage, a folding table of soda cans sweating in the June heat. She had been at this school since ninth grade and she recognized nearly every face, which was the problem, because she kept noticing the faces that were not there.

"Where's Marcus?" she asked Priya, who was stacking cups with the efficiency of someone avoiding conversation.

"Marcus who? Oh. Yeah." Priya flattened a cup into the stack. "He left sophomore year. Moved, I think."

"He was in my algebra class." Isabella could still see him hunched at the back desk, chewing his pen cap into plastic shreds. She had lent him notes once, or he had lent her some; she couldn't remember which direction the debt ran, only that they had never settled it.

Her brother Marco appeared behind her with his phone out, belligerent the way he got when he'd had two beers and wanted to argue about something, anything, preferably with family. "You know half the kids who started ninth grade with you aren't here tonight," he said. "Statistically."

"That's not statistics, that's a backyard."

"I looked it up for a paper. The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in 2021-22." He said it in his quoting voice, the one he used to litigate dinner-table disputes into surrender. "Your cohort. The whole country's. Thirteen out of every hundred just aren't in this picture."

"Then go find someone else's picture to ruin." She walked toward the lawn chairs, but the number came with her, the way a song does. Eighty-seven percent. She tried it against her own memories like a key against a lock: Tanisha, gone by October of freshman year, no goodbye. Devon, who'd been there in June and gone by September. The two girls who used to laugh in the stairwell until the laughing stopped. She had assumed, at the time, that they had simply dissolved, that some people were the substrate of a class, the layer underneath that everything else got built on and no one thought to mention. It had never occurred to her to count them.

She found her phone and scrolled to a message from December of junior year, from Tanisha, the only one she'd ever traded numbers with. She read it again where the string lights didn't quite reach.

Hey. Saw your photo from the choir thing. You looked happy. I'm at Heights now, it's fine, smaller. I keep meaning to write more but every time I start it sounds like an apology and I don't know what I'd be apologizing for. Anyway. You were one of the good ones. That's all.

Isabella had answered with a heart emoji and then nothing, because she hadn't known what to say either, and then a year had gone by like water through a fence. Tonight she sat with the phone in her lap and drafted three replies and deleted them, because each one tried to litigate the past into a verdict: I should have noticed. You should have told me. Nobody was wrong. The last one felt truest and also flattest, a verdict that closed the case without anyone testifying.

Priya came and dropped into the chair beside her, holding out a can of root beer as a truce. "You're doing the math face."

"It's not a face."

"You're doing it about Marcus, and Tanisha, and probably that whole missing thirteen percent." Priya popped her own can. "I do it too. I keep thinking graduation is a photo, and I keep noticing who got cropped out. But my mom says some of them graduated somewhere else, some moved, some are doing a fifth year. Thirteen percent just means they didn't finish with us. It doesn't say what happened to them."

"Your mom says a lot of things." But Isabella felt the number loosen its grip, or shift it. Eighty-seven percent was a fact, and the fact was quiet about the rest. It didn't say who had struggled and who had simply gone somewhere with better weather. It didn't say which of them, standing under these particular lights, was the lucky one and which was only the one still standing where the photograph was being taken. She wanted to hold both things at once, the luck and the loss, without letting either one erase the other, and she could feel the seam between them flexing every time she tried.

She typed a fourth reply to Tanisha, slowly, and this time she didn't delete it. It said: We graduated tonight and someone said a number and I thought of you immediately, not as a number. You were in my algebra class and you explained the coin problems better than the teacher did. I don't know where you are now. If you want, tell me. If you don't, that's okay too. She read it twice, thumb hovering over send.

Across the yard someone had turned the music up and a boy she'd known since seventh grade was dancing badly on purpose, and Marco was arguing with Dev's father about baseball, and the lights swung a little in a wind that had just come up.

She pressed send, watched the message lift off the ground, and put the phone face-down on her knee, still warm, and looked up at the yard full of everyone who had made it to a folding table in June.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In a standard repayment mortgage, early monthly payments go mostly toward interest, and later payments go mostly toward paying down the amount borrowed.
story:
The office smelled of toner and the lemon polish Mr. Aduba used on the counters every morning, and by the second week of her summer job Laura had learned to tell the time by the door. Ten o'clock brought the renters, clutching printouts, asking whether the deposit on a two-bedroom was really one month's rent plus a fee, and whether they would get any of it back if the blinds were already bent when they moved in. Two o'clock brought the buyers, quieter people who sat across from Mr. Aduba's desk with bank statements folded into squares, talking about down payments as if the words were fragile. Laura filed their paperwork, marked the keys in, made coffee, and listened.

Her own problem sat in her bag all afternoon: a letter from the housing office at the college she'd start in September, listing the dorm fee next to a smaller figure for sharing an off-campus apartment with three strangers. Her mother had said, over dinner, that they'd work it out, and then changed the subject to her aunt's knees, and Laura had understood that "work it out" meant she was supposed to work it out.

On Thursday her cousin Denise came in at four, still in her hospital scrubs, carrying a folder she dropped on the counter like something hot. "Five years," she said. "Five years of paying every single month, and I looked it up today and I still owe almost exactly what I borrowed. Where did the money go, Laura? Tell me where it went."

Mr. Aduba, who was phlegmatic about nearly everything, including burst pipes and a tenant who once kept goats, looked up from his screen. "Standard repayment loan," he said. "The early payments go mostly to interest." He turned back to his screen, as if that settled it, and for him it had.

Denise hadn't heard it that way before either. "So the bank takes its share first," she said slowly, "and only later does the money actually start bringing down what I owe."

Laura pulled the amortization sheet out of Denise's folder and ran her finger down the columns, curious now in spite of herself. The monthly number never changed, but its two halves shifted as the years went by, the interest slice shrinking and the other slice growing, until near the end nearly everything went to the borrowed amount itself. It was like watching a tide change direction so slowly you had to mark the waterline to prove it. She thought of her mother's old joke that the universe was patient because it could afford to be.

"Meanwhile I've been renting," Laura said, mostly to herself, "and I understood that part. You pay, you live there, the money's gone, and the deposit is the only piece that might circle back to you if you leave the place clean." She looked up. "I thought buying was the opposite. Money in, house yours. Nobody told me it's a long argument with the bank first, and for the first stretch the bank wins every month."

Denise laughed, a short, tired sound. "You'll be a freshman and you already prognosticate better than my loan officer." She squared the folder against the counter. "At least now I know the payments weren't wasted. They were just, what's the word, front-loaded."

Mr. Aduba slid a listing across the desk to a couple by the window, and the office hummed with its usual throughput of phone calls, key tags, and people carrying their futures around in envelopes. Laura photocopied the amortization sheet and folded it next to the housing letter in her bag, then sat at the front desk and did the arithmetic she'd been avoiding. Dorm fee times eight semesters. Off-campus rent times the same months, minus her share of a deposit she might never see again, plus a bus pass. The two totals sat near each other, close enough that the difference wouldn't decide anything by itself. What she couldn't price was quieter: whether she wanted to learn a city through a landlord's rules or through a roommate's dishes in the sink.

She understood something else, too, though it was less comfortable. Denise's payments hadn't vanished; they had gone somewhere, just not where Denise had pictured, and Laura liked knowing that the system had a logic even when it wasn't her logic. What she couldn't yet say was whether the logic was fair. Maybe the bank deserved its interest for lending the money at all, and maybe that was exactly the kind of sentence people said when the money wasn't theirs. She held both possibilities open the way you hold two keys, trying each in the same lock.

At closing time she wiped the counter, switched off the printer, and pulled the folded paper out again. On the back of the amortization sheet, in the margin, she wrote the dorm number, the rent number, and then, underneath, a small question mark that she didn't try to answer. Denise knocked on the glass from the parking lot, holding up her car keys through the window, and Laura clipped the page into her notebook, waved back, and went to lock the front door.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
The video arrived at 11:40 on a Tuesday night, forwarded from Dex with three fire emojis and the caption "bro look at this NOW." It showed a shopping mall in flames, smoke rolling against a sky the color of dishwater, people running with their jackets over their mouths. A caption in the corner gave a city and yesterday's date. Loic was alone in the living room, his mother asleep down the hall, and his thumb hovered over the forward arrow for the group chat before he noticed that his own heartbeat had picked up, as though the fire were something happening to him.

He sent it. Fourteen people received it in the next ninety seconds, and the replies stacked up fast, the little word bubbles portending a night of outrage. Dajah wrote "this is terrifying." Someone Loic barely knew from his sister's graduation wrote "what is WRONG with people." Loic typed "exactly" and felt the warm certainty of agreeing with everyone at once, the feeling he would later recognize as the cheapest thing he owned.

Then Nadia replied, three minutes later, with a screenshot. "This photo is old," she wrote. "It's been online since like 2017." She had run the still frame through something called TinEye, a reverse image search engine, and she'd sorted the results with the oldest first, which showed her when the image first appeared online, years before yesterday. Loic read the message twice. The fire emojis in his own forward suddenly looked insouciant, the seal of someone who had cared only about being first.

He didn't apologize right away. First he argued, because the first feeling is always that the correction is an attack. "The video format is different," he typed. "Someone re-uploaded it, so maybe it's new footage of the same thing." Nadia sent a link. He sat in the lamplight of the living room, the TV off, his mother's magazines fanned on the coffee table, and opened his laptop on the arm of the couch.

He dragged the frame into the search bar himself. He didn't want to take her word for it; he had decided at some point that year, without announcing it, that he was going to be a person who checked things, a small-time autodidact with a laptop and a grudge against being fooled. The results loaded, and he found the oldest-first option and clicked it, and there was the same smoke, the same dishwater sky, dated years back, on sites he'd never heard of, some of them dead now, the page still standing like a burned building left standing.

He typed an apology into the group chat. It felt insufficient and he sent it anyway. "I shared something fake," he wrote. "The photo's from years ago. Sorry, everyone, check before you forward." A couple of people replied with thumbs. Dajah wrote "good looking out." Someone else wrote "lol it's not that deep," and Loic sat with that for a while, the possibility that it wasn't, that he had turned a Tuesday night into a seminar nobody had enrolled in.

He called Nadia instead of texting, because some things you want to hear in a voice. "How'd you even know to do that," he asked. She was folding laundry, he could hear the fabric. "My cousin got burned during the election," she said. "Shared a thing, got quoted at a family dinner, spent a year being the cautionary tale." She laughed a little. "TinEye's been around since 2008, so it's not like it's a secret. People just don't use it."

He told her he'd run the oldest-first sort himself, that he'd seen the earliest result with his own eyes, and she said "then you did it right." It was a small compliment and he held on to it harder than he meant to. After they hung up he scrolled back through the group chat, past his fire emojis, past the fourteen forwards, and found that two people had sent the video on after his correction, probably without reading up that far. He couldn't reach those threads. He knew that now, and it didn't portend anything good, it was just true. He closed the laptop and sat in the quiet living room, then picked up his phone and opened his sister's chat, where the video sat unsent, and typed: "Before you share anything, there's a thing you should see."

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 1990 follow-up of Mischel's preschoolers found that those who had waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers.
story:
The lab smelled like wet dirt and coffee, which Kyle decided was what a real science lab should smell like, even if the posters on the wall were about something he'd never heard of before this spring: the soil microbiome, all the fungi and bacteria living in a handful of forest floor. Dr. Okafor had taken him on as a summer mentee after his chemistry teacher sent an email Kyle hadn't even known was being written. Now he sat at a stool beside the fume hood, pipetting liquid into little tubes with hands that were steadier than he expected, while his phone sat face-down in his backpack and vibrated against a spiral notebook.

He didn't check it. He had a rule about that, invented twenty minutes ago.

The vibration was almost certainly Mr. Duvall from the landscaping company, calling to confirm whether Kyle could start Monday. Fourteen dollars an hour, forty hours a week, all summer, real money by August. The research position here, by contrast, was unpaid, and its rewards were the kind adults praised in a language Kyle privately thought of as rain-word, vague and falling everywhere at once. Experience. Connections. A line on an application.

"So you're the new one," said Priya, a lanky girl in a college hoodie who had wandered over from the greenhouse bay. She watched him pipette with an expression of polite horror. "You're pushing too hard. Let the drop fall on its own."

Kyle eased his thumb. A drop detached, tidy as a bead.

"What are you doing this summer?" she asked. "Here, or the thing?"

"The thing?"

"Some people do the summer program and then leave in July for jobs." She shrugged. "Dr. Okafor pretends not to mind. My mom thinks I'm insane for staying. She keeps bringing up this study. The marshmallow one. Little kids, one treat now or two if they wait." Priya rolled her eyes toward the ceiling. "She read that a 1990 follow-up of those preschoolers found the kids who'd waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers. So now every time I choose homework over a shift at the pool, she's smug about it for a week."

"Wait, they followed them for years? Actual years?"

"Twelve or something. I don't know. My mom tells it like a fable." Priya drifted back toward the greenhouse, and Kyle stood there with his pipette suspended, a drop trembling at its tip.

He wanted to dismiss it. It was a fable, obviously, the kind of thing adults used to make patience sound like virtue instead of what it usually was, standing around while other people got the good seats. One afternoon with a marshmallow couldn't reach across a decade and grab a number out of some kid's future. But then, the landscaping job was also a single afternoon's decision, and everyone acted as if it would reach forward and grab his. Mr. Duvall had said the crew he joined this summer often came back every year through college, which sounded either like loyalty or like a trap, depending on the hour at which Kyle thought about it.

At the break, he used the old desktop in the lab's corner, the one with the screen the color of weak tea. The library database gave him the study without much digging: preschoolers, treats, the waiting, and then, in a 1990 follow-up, the longer waiters tending toward higher SAT scores as teenagers. He read it twice. The word that snagged him was "tended." Not guaranteed, not always, just leaned, the way a slope leans. He tried to recalibrate around it, to hold both things at once: that a choice made in one afternoon seemed to lean on a person for years, and that leaning wasn't deciding. Somewhere under all that was the fact that no one had ever offered him a second marshmallow for waiting. Waiting, in his house, had just been waiting.

Because that was the part he hadn't told Dr. Okafor, or Priya, or anyone. The word he kept behind his teeth. His mother had started picking up extra shifts in March, and the second-shift differential didn't cover what the hospital had started sending in envelopes she left on the microwave, turned address-side down. Kyle had done the arithmetic on the bus. Fourteen dollars an hour, forty hours, eleven weeks. He could carry the fall by himself, the way she'd carried everything since June of last year. That was the calculation sitting in his backpack, buzzing.

Dr. Okafor came back from the staff room with two cups of tea and offered him one, and when Kyle took it she became unexpectedly effusive about his pipetting, saying he had good hands, that good hands were rarer than good grades, that the bacteria in sample seven had done something under the microscope this morning that she wanted to show him. She leaned over the scope and adjusted the fine focus, and the screen filled with a smear of life, threads and dots moving through soil water like a slow city. "This biome," she said, tapping the screen with one finger, "has been developing in that jar since February. Every day it becomes more itself. You cannot rush it and you cannot skip ahead and see what it will be in August."

Kyle looked at the jar. Then, in a way that felt like stepping off a curb he'd been standing on all day, he took his phone out of the backpack. The screen said one missed call, one voicemail. He stood in the doorway of the lab where the dirt smell was strongest and pressed the phone to his ear, and Mr. Duvall's voice came through flat and cheerful, saying the crew slot was his if he wanted it, saying to call back by five, saying no rush, kid, it's your summer.

Behind him Dr. Okafor was still bent over the microscope, patient as soil. He looked at the clock above the sink, then at the screen, where the threads kept moving through their dark, unfinished city. He dialed.

"Mr. Duvall? It's Kyle." He watched a single bead form at the tip of his abandoned pipette, hanging there, holding on. "I need to ask you something before I answer."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Percent yield is the actual mass of product obtained divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
story:
The kitchen smelled of Grandpa Walt's coffee, bitter and old, and Jordan set his shoebox of alum crystals on the table between the sugar bowl and the window geranium. The largest crystal sat on a folded paper towel, blue-white and faceted, and beside it his lab notebook lay open to the page where he'd weighed everything twice.

"They're smaller than the ones in your photograph," Grandpa said, turning the box with one finger. He had the saturnine face of a man who had spent forty years underground in the gypsum mine, and he looked at the crystal the way he looked at most things, as if it had already disappointed him somewhere.

"That's the problem," Jordan said. "I started with twenty-five grams of alum. That's potassium aluminum sulfate dodecahydrate, molar mass four hundred seventy-four grams per mole. So I divide, and I get about zero point zero five three moles of the stuff, and since it comes back out of solution as the same compound, the theoretical yield is twenty-five grams. But the crystals only weigh twenty-one point four grams." He slid the notebook across. "I lost almost four grams somewhere."

Grandpa studied the figures without touching them. "And what do you call that. The number you're after."

Jordan had written the division on the back of an envelope that morning, on the bus, and he'd been carrying the answer around all day like a stone in his pocket. "Percent yield. You take the actual mass you got, divide by the theoretical yield, multiply by a hundred. Mine's eighty-five point six percent." He said it flat, because the number still embarrassed him. At the regional fair in March, a judge had asked him for it, and he'd stood there with his mouth open, having never computed it at all.

"You were supposed to win that thing," Grandpa said. It wasn't a question. Two springs ago they had driven down to the fair together in the truck with the rusted wheel well, and Jordan had taken second, and on the drive home Grandpa had said the judges wouldn't know a decent crystal if it fell on them. That was the last good stretch between them. Afterward came the silent autumn, when Jordan stopped visiting because Grandpa had told his father, at Thanksgiving, that a boy who spent his weekends washing glassware was wasting the only youth he'd get. His father, who could pontificate for a full hour on the dignity of manual labor without ever having held a shovel he wasn't photographing, had returned fire, and Jordan had spent the holiday in the car with the radio on.

"Some of it's still in solution," Jordan said. "The water holds a little alum even when it's cold. Some stuck to the filter paper. Some probably splashed when I poured." He tapped the envelope. "But I can't prove which. That's the part that got me. I know how much I lost, not where."

Grandpa got up and refilled his cup, and the chair scraped the linoleum in the way Jordan had memorized without meaning to. In the mine, Grandpa had said once, you measured what came up the shaft, and what didn't come up, you didn't guess at. You just dug differently next week. Jordan had thought that was a hard way to live. He wasn't sure now. His own method had been to calculate until the numbers matched, and when they didn't match, to decide the scale was wrong.

"Eighty-five and a half," Grandpa said, sitting back down. "In the mill that would've been a good week."

"Dr. Okafor says above ninety is excellent for a first recrystallization." Jordan heard himself and laughed a little. "But she's not the one who has to write it on the poster."

"So write it." Grandpa pushed the envelope back toward him. "Write that you know what you got and you know what it should've been. A man who hides the shortfall hides it the second time too."

Jordan looked at the crystal, at the small perfect faces of it, grown atom by atom from the water in a mason jar on his desk while he slept. He had wanted, all spring, to be the boy whose numbers came out clean. What he had instead was a number with a gap in it, and the honest sentence that the gap was real and its cause was not. He picked up the pen and began printing neatly beneath the division: actual mass divided by theoretical yield, times one hundred, equals 85.6 percent.

"Next year," he said, "I'll cool it slower. Filter it twice." He glanced up. "If I'm still welcome to use the garage for the evaporation dishes."

Grandpa turned the crystal once more in the light from the window, and the facets threw small bright coins across the tablecloth.

"Wash them when you're done," he said. "Both of you. You can tell your father that."
